Mr. Speaker, on the 28th day of May, the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) addressed to me a letter which I desire to read to the House and which is as follows.-.
Might I respectfully ask the right hon. the Prime Minister to speak a little louder? We cannot hear one word back here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had said that on the 28th day of May the hon. the Minister of Public Works addressed to me a letter which I desire to read to the House and which is as follows:
Office of the Minister Of Public Works.
Ottawa, May 28, 1917. My dear Sir Robert:

Some time in the summer of nineteen sixteen, the present Government of Manitoba appointed a Commissioner, Mr. A. C. Galt, to make investigation and to report to them with regard; to the construction of the Manitoba Agricultural College. This work was undertaken and a very small proportion done while I was Minister of Public Works for that province. Mr. Galt has made two reports-one some time last January and the other two or three days ago. In these reports 'he has chosen to reflect on my conduct as such minister, and it is only as regards those portions of the reports in which he so reflects that I feel justified in drawing thel matter to your attention.

While making his investigation on the subjects covered by his first report, Mr. Galt telegraphed me to Ottawa on September 12 last, informing me of certain evidence which he evidently regarded as requiring answer on my part. I at once went to Winnipeg and appeared before him and gave full explanation of the subject covered by his telegram and answered all questions put to me. It was manifest to me then from Mr. Galt's demeanour and remarks that he purposed sparing no effort and rejecting no means, however unfair, of doing me all the injury in his power. I therefore, from that point forward, took little or no interest in the proceedings of his Commission, being absolutely certain not only that my own conduct in the premises had been straightforward and in the public interest, but that, though it would he a waste of time to make any attempt to Influence the purpose of Mr. Commissioner Galt, there would be no difficulty later in exposing and establishing before any fair and competent tribunal both the true facts of the case and the malice of this commissioner. I did, however, subsequently inform Mr. Galt that I was prepared, though in Ottawa, to answer any summons in the same way a* if it were served on me in Manitoba.	,
As regards the proceedings subsequent to the first report, and as regards the subjects covered by the second report, in respect to which Mr. Galt is pleased to reflect on my public conduct, you will he surprised to learn-I say this knowing that you are not acquainted with Mr. Galt-that I was never informed by the Commissioner, directly or indirectly, of any statements in evidence affecting me in the slightest degree, nor was I offered any opportunity whatever of making explanation or defence. It is quite true that no explanation or defence, however complete or however substantiated, would have affected in the least Mr. Galt's determination, hut this fact cannot be offered as an excuse on his part for abandoning and indeed prostituting the most elementary principle of British justice-that it is a fact, however, does, I think, fully establish the predetermination and malice of the Commissioner.
As soon as I was informed of the contents of each report, I made full and public denial of every allegation contained in them, affecting myself. This denial I now reaffirm.
I believe I am entitled to a full and fair investigation by a tribunal of high standing of all matters contained in these reports, reflecting in any way on my public conduct. Though I have not yet been able to obtain a copy of the evidence, I cannot believe that any evidence could have been given substantiating the reports so far as they allege breach of duty on my part. I ask that such a tribunal be appointed in order that it may be known whether there was such evidence, and if so, to make full and complete inquiry and report as to whether, if any such evidence was given, the same was true.
Yours sincerely,
R. Rogers.
To that letter I gave the following reply on the 30th day of May:
Ottawa, 30th May, 1917.
Dear Mr. Rogers,
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 2Sth instant I 'have taken into consideration the action which you request with respect to the

reflections upon your conduct as a member of the Provincial Executive of Manitoba, which are set forth in the reports of Commissioner Galt. I shall bring your request to the attention of Council forthwith so that your representations and the course which should be taken with regard to the matter may be considered by all the members of the Government.
Yours faithfully.
The Honourable
Robert Rogers, M.P.,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
The subject was taken up and considered in council, with the result that it was referred to the Minister of Justice, who yesterday presented a report to council upon which an Order in Council has been passed and approved by His Excellency. I shall now read that Order in Council:
Certified copy of a Report of the Committee of the Privy Council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 6th June, 1917.
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a Report dated 4th June, 1917, from the Minister of Justice, stating that the Honourable Mr. Justice Galt of Manitoba, who was appointed a Commissioner by the Lieutenant Governor of Manitoba on 15th July, 1916, to investigate and report upon certain matters of concern to the local Government, has, as the Minister of Justice is informed, in pursuance of his said Commission made two reports, the first dated 26th January last, and the second, dated 25th May, by which reports the Commissioner makes certain findings or observations reflecting upon the honour or integrity of the Honourable Robert Rogers, presently _ Minister of Public Works of Canada, in con-' nection with the said matters above referred to and his actions in regard thereto, at a time when he was Minister of Public Works of the said Province of Manitoba, and that Mr. Rogers avers that all such findings and observations and the said reports In so far as they in anywise affect him prejudicially are unjustified in fact and not upheld or established by the evidence or facts in proof before the Commissioner.
Mr. Rogers also complains of lack of notice, and that as to some of the findings in question he was not afforded an opportunity to give or present evidence before the Commissioner, and moreover he challenges the impartiality and intent of the Commissioner upon the matters under consideration so far as they affect Mr. Rogers. In these circumstances Mr. Rogers asks for a full and fair investigation by a tribunal of high standing of all matters contained in the aforesaid reports reflecting in any -way upon his public conduct.
The minister being of the opinion that the situation as thus presented invites further consideration recommends that the Honourable Sir Ezekiel McLeod, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, and the Honourable Louis Tellier, a retired Judge of the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec, be appointed Commissioners under Part 1 of the Inquiries Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1916, Chapter 104, for the purpose of reviewing and considering the evidence taken before the said Commissioner Galt in the execution of his commission aforesaid, and his said reports and findings thereon, and of reporting for the information of Your Excellency in Council whether, there was evidence before the said Commissioner Galt to sustain or support the findings of said Commissioner as set forth in his said reports in so far as they reflect upon or prejudicially affect the honour or integrity of Mr. Rogers or the honesty of his dealings or transactions, the said hereby appointed Commissioners to have power should they find that there is any such evidence, to make such further inquiry and take such further and additional evidence as may to them appear necessary for the purpose of enabling them to determine and report upon the truth or falsity of the evidence so tby them found, any further evidence so taken and the determination of said hereby named Commissioners thereon to be also reported; and that the said Honourable Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Honourable Louis Tellier as such Commissioners shall moreover have all the powers in the execution of their said Commission which are mentioned, enumerated or provided for by the said Part 1 of the Inquiries Act and the Act amending the same of 2 George V. Chapter 28, intituled "An Act to amend the Inquiries Act".
The Committee concur in the foregoing and submit the same for'approval.
Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
There is nothing further to add except that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) has requested of me that, pending the investigation, he shall be relieved of all administrative duties in connection with the Department of Public Works, and that the administration of the department shall be taken over by myself or by some other minister, and I have acceded to that request.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER: By your leave, Mr. Speaker, 1 think the correspondence and the Order in Council which has just been submitted to the House require some comments on my part. I would say that the letter addressed by the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to the Prime Minister is absolutely derogatory to the honour of the bench of this country.
Hear, hear.

The letter
refers to Mr. Justice Galt, not as Mr. Justice Galt but as "Mr. Galt." Mr. Justice Galt acted, not in his capacity as a judge, but he was selected-as the hon. gentlemen who have just been named in the Order in Council, Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Hon. Louis Tellier, have been selected-on account of his judicial capacity. It is to be remembered, Sir, and it cannot be forgotten on this occasion, that the complaint of the Minister of Public Works of unfairness by Mr. Justice Galt to him arose largely, if not altogether, and I would say altogether, from the insult which was poured upon the

head of Mr. Justice Galt by the Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Public Works was called upon to give evidence before the commissioner. He had the right to be summoned, and he appeared. And, Sir, in the public press and in his evidence to Mr. Justice Galt's face he called him a grafter.
Hear, hear.

For what
reason was he called a grafter? Because he accepted duties similar to those which have just been delegated to Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Hon. Louis Tellier, justices of the High Court. If Mr. Justice Galt was a grafter-which I resent, I do not know Mr. Justice Galt, I never met him in my life; he is a judge of the bench, that is all I know-but if he can be called a grafter for having accepted the duties which he discharged, Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Hon. Louis Tellier can also be called grafters equally; there is no difference. Now, Sir, the hon. Minister of Public Works asks that gentlemen of high standing shall be appointed to make a further inauiry. The tribunal which is toeing constituted by the Government to investigate this matter is of no higher or of no lower standing than the commission which was presided over by Mr. Justice Galt; it is exactly the same. I do not know Mr. Justice Galt, but I understand that he is a judge of integrity, in good standing in his profession, and that his honour has never before been impugned. Before he was appointed to the Bench he was not active in either political party. Under these circumstances, if any new tribunal is to try the Minister of Pulblio Works,' it should be a committee of this House. There are two methods of making public investigations, either by a committee of this House, the High Court of Parliament, or *by members of the Bench, who are selected because of their legal standing and because they are supposed, by the very character of their office, to be above reproach. If the report is to be condemned because the commission was presided over by a judge of the Supreme Court, the new inquiry should not toe carried out by a commission of the same kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not disposed to discuss the character or qualifications of Mr. Justice Galt on this or any other occasion, unless a necessity which I cannot now foresee should arise. As I understand it, the judges who are to perform this duty are not to accept fee or [Sii Wilfrid Laurier.]	_
honorarium for it. My right hon. friend challenges the action we have taken and challenges the reflections which have been made upon Mr. Justice Galt in the letter written to me from the Minister of Public Works. I should like to remind him that on a certain occasion one of his colleagues who sits beside him used infinitely stronger language, if my memory is correct, with regard to Mr. Justice Landry of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, and he did so without any reproof from my right hon. friend. 'I am perfectly willing to contrast the action which we have taken in this matter with that which my right hon. friend took on that occasion. Findings had been made by a commission of which Mr. Justice Landry was a member. Those findings reflected seriously upon a member of my right hon. friend's Government. The matter was brought to the attention of Par-[DOT] liament, and it was urged toy a motion in this House that such a finding should not be disregarded. My right hon. friend ignored the whole matter and voted down the motion, the precise words of which I have not before me; no consideration to the finding was given toy him, and the then Minister of Public Works retained his position in the Government and continued to administer the affairs of his department. It seemed to me, when the matter was brought to my attention by the present Minister of Public Works, that such a course as was on that occasion pursued by* my right hon. friend could not be followed pr sanctioned with advantage to the public interest. I thought it my duty, therefore, to comply with the request made by the Minister of Public Works and to entrust the examination of this evidence and any further hearing that might be desired, to two members of the Judicial Bench, one cf whom is on the Bench at present and the other of whom has retired. Both are absolutely above reproach. I may add that the Minister of Public Works informs me that he is not acquainted with either of these two judges, and that, so far as he knows, he never met either one or the other of them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I see in the morning papers a report which reads as follows:
Ottawa, June 5.-An extraordinary position of affairs was revealed in a return made this

evening In a volume of correspondence between the iSergeant-at-Arms of the House of Commons and Hon. Albert Sevigny, and between the Sergeant-at-Arms and the Justice Department, with regard to a quantity of valuable effects removed from the Speaker's chambers at the House of Commons early in 1916 by Hon. Mr. Sevigny during his tenure? of office as Speaker. It appeared that Hon. Mr. Sevigny had removed a number of handsome pictures and works of art
-which, by the way, is not true.
a Viotrola and a quantity of high priced records, with other ornaments and furniture and had them sent to Quebec.
Col Smith wrote Hon. Mr. Sevigny several times'apparently without getting any response. He then wrote a sharp letter to Hon. Mr. Sevigny, pointing out that he must know that these goods should be in the custody of himself as Sergeant-at-Arms, and that he was responsible for them. Yet in face of repeated requests Hon. Mr. Sevigny had continued to retain them, etc.
This article, published in the Montreal Gazette this morning, is absolutely false; there is nothing in the papers which were submitted to the. House yesterday to sustain those assertions. The facts are as follows. As everybody knows, the Speaker's Chambers were destroyed by fire last year when I was Speaker of the House of Commons-and, by the way, I may be permitted to say that my monetary losses as a result of the fire amounted to about $1,200. Last year when the House prorogued as there were no quarters for the Speaker, I asked the officers of the House if there would be any objection to sending to Quebec certain effects which were in Ottawa at the disposal of the Speaker of the House of Commons during the Tecess. No objection was raised at the time by any of the officers of the House, and, accordingly, instructions were given that certain effects be sent to Quebec. A list of those effects w as made by the Serjoait-at-Arms, and they were sent to Quebec by the Serjeant-at-Arms. On January 8 of this year, I was invited to join the Cabinet and the next day I had to go to Dorchester for my reelection. I was there until the end of January. When I came back I was sick for several days, and when I came to my office in Ottawa I was very busy with my departmental business. When I w.as asked for the first time by the Serjeant-at-Arms to .send back those effects, I told hi.m, in a letter of which a copy was submitted to the House yesterday, that I would send them as soon as I should be back in Quebec. I wrote a second letter to the Serjeant-at-Arms in which I repeated that. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that my intention never was to keep those effects and
that they .were returned to the Serjeant-at-Arms in perfect order.

Windsor, June 5.-Information has been received here by local members of the internal revenue and other branches of the Civil Service to the effect that within a short time-a few weeks at most-the Government will announce a plan for compulsory retirement of all civil servants who have been in the service more than thirty-five years, their places to he filled with returned soldiers who are unfit by reason of wounds and illness from filling their ordinary vocations.

On motion of Hon. Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 47, to facilitate certain financial arrangements between the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and for other purposes, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the chair.
On the Preamble:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: As I explained upon the introduction of this Bill to the House, its object is to enable the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to lend its credit to the Imperial Treasury by issuing collateral trust bonds payable in currency-

maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In what currency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Canadian, United . States, or British, against outstanding securities of the company, payable as to principal and interest in sterling, which have been, ot which may be, acquired by the Imperial Government. Legislation is necessary because the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will do this to facilitate the financing by the Imperial Treasury and not for its own railway purposes. I am advised that the Canadian Pacific Railway .Company has statutory powers to issue

these new securities, if issued for railway purposes, but as the purpose is to facilitate the Imperial financing, it is necessary to obtain legislative authority to issue these collateral trust bonds, which are to be delivered to the Imperial Government in exchange for sterling securities which it has acquired or may acquire on the London market. The transaction is necessitated by reason of the exchange situation to which I have frequently referred in this House. The British Government has been acquiring sterling securities in London. Those sterling securities have in the past been used as collateral to loans which the Imperial Government has been making in New York for the purpose of supplying funds to meet its expenditures in the United States. Among other securities which have been or which will be acquired are the sterling securities of the Canadian Pacific Bailway Company, and of certain of the companies whose lines are leased by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, principally, I may say, the four per cent debenture stock of the Canadian Pacific. The position, therefore, is that the Imperial Government has acquired this stock and other securities. As these securities are payable in sterling, they are not available as collateral or for sale on this side of the Atlantic, and the Imperial treasury has requested the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to issue collateral trust bonds in exchange for these sterling debentures, the collateral trust bonds to be payable in currency so that they may be used for an issue on this side of the Atlantic, or as collateral for such an issue. I have already explained to the House that no such issue is an immediate prospect, and I have' stated further-and this has been brought to my knowledge-that although no such loan is in prospect, the Imperial Government has requested the Canadian Pacific Company to proceed with this legislation, in order that, should occasion arise, this power may be available.

If these bonds were payable in currency of the Dominion of Canada, then the company would have the right to pay in paper currency, in which case the bond would not have the same value as if the payment was made in gold. But of course this is a matter of internal arrangement, and the company are the best judges.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) Bill No. 55, to amend the Penny Bank Act, was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 1-withdrawals for investment in Government securities, and application of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This legislation
is to enable the Penny Banks to invest their funds in Dominion Government securities subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance. These banks are voluntary organizations whose object is to encourage savings by school children, and others of slender means. They are not banks under the Bank Act, and deposits by any one individual are limited to $300. At present under the Act relating to Penny Banks their funds must be deposited with the Post Office Savings Bank, and interest is allowed at the rate of 4 per cent per annum under a special arrangement with the Government. We have been requested to authorize the banks to invest in the Dominion War Loan issues, and as there seems to be no objection I have introduced this legislation. There is this safeguard, that any such investments are subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance, and of course the security is just as good as if the funds were invested in the Post Office Saving , Bank.

The bonds are to be
deposited with the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, that is a
safeguard that my hon. friend will find in the Bill.
How many of these banks are there in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two,
the head office of the larger bank being in Toronto, with branches in thirty-four centres. The otheT bank is a smaller organization at Chicoutimi. The Penny Bank of Toronto has on deposit in the Post Office Savings Bank $370,OCO, and the Penny Bank of Chicoutimi $13,000.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
Grant to the National Battlefields Commission, $52,100.

['The statement made by the Minister of Labour as to the information he was gathering with regard to cold storage warehouses was so diffuse and so voluminous that I was not able to gather what he was really doing, and I think we should thoroughly understand just what is being done before this item is passed.

Has anything been done since last year in this matter? Is it proposed to add anything in the way of improvements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Not at present. The understanding is that the present works should be maintained, but that no new works shall be undertaken.
For maintenance of the National Battlefields Park, $46,200.
How is this to be expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should have to get the report of the commission, in order to give my hon. friend full information. I am not able to speak from memory. We have provided the amount requested by the commissioners for maintenance, on the understanding that new works would not be undertaken, but that they would do their best to maintain the works at present existing. That does not mean that we should not complete the works, if it were found more convenient to do so, having regard to the financial situation.

I have no
fault to find with the commission. It is a fine commission, and I am sure that every dollar will be spent economically, but I would like to let the item stand.
Item stands.

Has the Battlefields Commission jurisdiction over the national monuments? I understand there are certain places in Canada where historical events have occurred, which are taken charge of by the Government?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This commission has not jurisdiction over that matter.

What particular
4 p.m. body has jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think any particular body has jurisdiction.

I saw a statement some time ago that certain portions of territory in the western part of Nova Scotia, for example the site of the original settlement of the-Acadians at Grand Pre, were to be taken over as a national park. Is that matter in contemplation by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no official knowledge of any such action. I think the report is probably premature.
Grant In aid of Canadian general council of the Boy Scouts' Association, $5,000.
How is that money expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By the Association, which has for its objects and purposes the Boy Scout movement. We pay the amount to the Association.
Is the Association numerous?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is very large, and has grown a great deal. How large it is, I am not prepared to say.
The grant is made to the Canadian general council of the Boy Scout Association. Is that a numerous body, and where is it located? Is it in Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that that item had better be allowed to stand. I apologize for not having information today. The Minister of Agriculture has just come in, and we will be glad to take up his estimates, and when we reach this item again I shall be able to explain it more fully.
Item stands.

Department of Agriculture-Patent record, $30,000.

Is this item for the
printing of those books which are distributed monthly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I think that it would be a good idea if the ministers would cut that item in two, and only print about one-tenth the number of books at present printed. They are scattered round broadcast, and I do not suppose that one person in a hundred who receives these books ever opens them. I have been getting them for about thirty years, and they are no good to me. Anybody who wants to get the information contained in the patent record can. get it on going to the Patent branch of the Department of Agriculutre. To my mind, it is one of the most useless bit's of expenditure undertaken by the Government.

There may be something in what my hon. friend says. That idea has been advanced a good many times in the last twenty years or so, and on the other side there have been a good many arguments advanced why it should be printed, and why the circulation should be as large as it is. These books are sent, free of charge, to the members of the Senate and the House of Commons and the libraries. Sixty-six different libraries in England get them, ninety-four libraries in Canada, fifty-four in the United States. There is an exchange list of seventy-nine and a Government free list of thirty-one, and the British colonies and foreign colonies, fifty-seven, free, making altogether 381.
How many are printed?
Twelve hundred copies per month. This amount includes all the necessary cuts, drawings, etc.

It seems to me that they are printed unreasonably often. Why could they not be printed quarterly or semiannually? It is not necessary, even for anybody who is interested in patent matters, that a list such as this should be printed every month. Twelve hundred copies a month, costing $30,000, means that we pay over $2 for each one of these books. I have been getting these books for thirteen years, and I have never had five cents of value out of them, because this is not in my line; I do not understand it; I am not interested. A great many members must be in the same position as I am. Sending it to libraries may be all right, but you might

cut the issue away down and it might he issued less frequently than monthly.
Do you suggest cutting out the copies to the members of the House and the Senate?
I would move that the members be cut off and the members of the Government also.
We will bear that suggestion in mind.
I think the suggestion is entitled to consideration. - It is very rarely that a member or a senator has occasion to refer to the list, and if he has occasion to refer to it he can get a copy.

The patent office is a profitable institution in the sense that last year the cash receipts amounted to $227,000, or $10,000 over those of any previous year; so that apart from the expense of the Patent Record and of the civil administration concerned with patents, there is still a very large amount credited to the Receiver General from the patent office. I shall be very glad to bear in mind what my hon. friend says about cutting down the issue of the Patent Record.

We have been long
enough in the House to know what a minister means when he says he will bear something in mind. He gets his estimates through and he never takes any action. But in that my hon. friend is not any worse than his colleagues or his predecessors.
That is hard upon ourselves.
It may be hard upon ourselves, but it is a fact nevertheless.

I am not competent to say at the moment whether all members and senators should have it or not. When I tell my hon. friend that I will bear his suggestion in mind, what I mean is that I would like to inform myself, by consulting the Deputy Commissioner of Patents as to the precise character of the objections to the proposal and to ascertain whether there might be something to be said on the other side. My hon. friend would not expect me to say offhand what should be done and therefore I was not at all hypocritical in saying that I would bear his suggestion in mind.

I imagine the deputy who gets an extra $1,000 on account of the patent branch would not like to see the expenditure cut down. I never knew a
deputy yet who was anxious to have the expenditure cut down. That depends on the minister. If it is going to be cut down my hon. friend will have to take hold with a strong hand and overrule his subordinates. This is one of the things in which economy might be practised without hurting anybody. Supposing we spend $15,000, instead of $30,000, issue these books once in three months and cut off a lot of the supply, the saving would be worth while.

I think there is a good deal in what my hon. friend says.. I would like, however, to feel satisfied that every one of my hon. friend's fellow members and senators took the same view. If that were the case, there would be no hesitation.

As one member who has been receiving this paper for a very long time, I can corroborate what my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) has said. I have never regarded it as anything else than a bulky nuisance coming to the office and which had to be thrown away.
Experimental Farms-Maintenance of Central Farm, and establishment and maintaining of additional branch Stations, $850,000.
This is practically the same vote as last year.

What is being done to find out how to handle the question of rust on wheat? Last year Canada lost about $100,000,000 and I understand that the average loss per annum in the United States is about $150,000,000. Last year was the first year in which we had a very general and severe loss of wheat from rust and it was only about the second time that we have had any serious infestation of rust in the West. I remember that ten or twelve years ago we had more or less rust but it was nothing like as severe as it was last year.

Yes. I understand that scientific men are finding out a good deal about it. I understand from one of the professors in Winnipeg that the rust spores can only be carried over from one year to another on a certain shrub, the barberry bush, and it appears that in the province of Manitoba there are only about 350 of these bushes. '	.

There are more than
that.

That is my information, although it may not be correct. This professor also stated that it was possible that

some other plant or shrub than the barberry might carry over the spores from one season to another, but 60 far all the research that has been made has failed to discover any such bush. I understand also that the spores are so extremely light that, for instance in an absolutely still room with the doors and windows all closed and with no current of an air, a spore will take an hour to fall a distance of four feet with the result that they can be carried hundreds of miles by the wind. It has been noticed that in the two seasons in which we havie^suf-fered badly from rust in the western provinces it has been after we have had a great deal of south wind, which has brought the spores up from the more southern part of the continent. I know that the American Government is spending a large amount of money in the effort to find out some tvay to handle this plague, and probably in the end something will be discovered by which we will be able to control it. I remember when smut was with us a very serious menace in the West and the cause of a loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars to the farmers. Now scientific men have discovered how to deal with smut, and the farmers are able to guard against it. I have no doubt that the same thing ivill occur with rust. It is such a very serious matter that I think the department would be justified in spending some money in the effort to guard against this disease.

I agree with everything my hon. friend has said in regard to rust, and the figures he has quoted of the losses caused by it are the same as the estimates we have had. As we considered it such a serious matter, we prepared some time ago for the erection of two field laboratories, one at Indian Head and one at Brandon, on our experimental farms. We were anxious to secure the very best man to take charge of this work, and I finally heard of Mr. W. P. Eraser, assistant professor of biology at Macdonald College, as being the most competent man on this continent in reference to diseases of this kind. I discussed the matter with Dr. Harrison, who was very loathe to lose Mr. Fraser, but I represented to him the importance of this investigation, and finally Dr. Harrison agreed, and Mr. Fraser entered our service at a fairly good' salary, and is now in charge of this branch of our work. I may say that when I applied to the American authorities in the effort to secure a first-class man, I was informed that I need not go outside of Canada as Mr. Fraser was the very best man on this con-

tinent. We have a number of very skilled men on fungus diseases in the department, as we have greatly enlarged this branch of our service during the past three or four years, but for this investigation we desired a man of pre-eminent ability, and I have every reason to believe that in Mr. Fraser we have secured such a man. I may say that we have printed 100,000 copies of a poster about two feet by three feet showing the disease in all its phases and giving the best methods of combatting it, so far as we know. This has been very generally distributed, and I hope my hon. friend has received a copy of it.
Where are the different stations to be located?

The vote always reads in this way. We allow a certain amount of leeway for the establishment of new stations. We are rather holding back in the matter since the war, with the expectation of strengthening and developing the work in existing stations and with the expectation also of the establishment of a considerable number of illustration stations. We have taken forty or fifty acres of the land of some progressive farmer in a certain district, and then, under our direction, he has carried out various methods of planting and handling his soil. I think that we supply seed to a certain extent. This has furnished an object lesson to all farmers in the district. I think, strictly speaking, it may be regarded as provincial work, but we took it up in 1914 owing to the drouth in Southern Alberta and Saskatchewan, because we had evidence there that a large number of the newer settlers had no scientific knowledge of the proper handling of the soil and the warding off of the danger of drouth. We have established something like thirty of these illustration stations. We have also made a start in Quebec, and have ten or twelve stations in that province, and one or two in the Maritime Provinces. We shall probably do a little more in that line this season. Whether we shall establish more experimental farms this year, I would not be prepared to say. We have a great number of places which are under the impression that they have been promised stations, or have had promises to look into the matter, and at the same time I think our work is sufficiently heavy, especially in view of the immediate necessities of the war, to cause a little halt in the establishment of experimental farms.

The minister is anxious to increase the production of the country.

Are the experimental stations in Quebec all over the province or in what localities are they?
The ones 'actually established are in Chateauguay, Drummond, Champlain, Bonaventure, Rimouski, Mis-sisquoi, Chicoutimi, Dor Chester, Vercheres and Labelle.

There are two experimental stations in the Peace river country, one -at Vermilion and one at Beaverlo'dge, two very important and very widely separated sections of the country. In view of the fact that the great Peace river country is now in process of development and is attracting the attention of settlers more than any other part of the prairie west, it is in the public interest that such experimental and illustrative work as has been carried on in these two localities should be amplified and extended so as to establish as thoroughly and .as rapidly as possible to what extent the climatic conditions prevailing in that country are adapted to agricultural production. The great possibilities of advantage in the establishing of these experimental farms or stations are most evident where a new country is in process of occupation and where everything in the line of agriculture is necessarily experimental. The experiments carried on by the Government at the general expense may be the means of saving enormous losses to the settlers in their work of development and corresponding losses to the country, which .benefits by their successes and loses by their failures. The Vermilion settlement .and experimetal station is three or four hundred miles further north than the city of Edmonton. There has been an agricultural settlement at that point for many years, and a large area of that district is reputed to he suitable for settlement. Vermilion is in the neighbourhood of north latitude 57, and it goes without saying that farming there may be subject to conditions not generally understood in latitudes below 49. While there has been a sufficiently continued and successful production at Vermilion to demonstrate the agricultural possibilities of that country, in the expansion of settlement throughout the possible agricultural area^the difficulties to be encountered might be successfplly solved in advance at a farm or station more fully equipped than the present station at Vermilion. I am not at all belittling the importance of the station or the work that it has done. But a new condition has arisen
through the railroad reaching Peace River town- and the establishing of regular steamboat communication on the river; Vermilion is within the reach of the pioneer settler as it was not two years ago. This condition justifies the amplification of the good work that has been carried on at the Vermilion station and the fuller development of that work by the department.
Somewhat the same argument applied to the work on Grande Prairie at Beaverlodge. The large, progressive and successful settlement on the Grande Prairie has been established only five or six years, and during so short a period the conditions can not have been tried out by the pioneer settlers to the fullest extent. I suggest, therefore, that on the Grande Pirairie, in the Beaver-lodge locality or elsewhere, it is in the public interest that the department amplify and develop the work that they are now carrying on, with a view of discovering and of demonstrating the agricultural possibilities of the Grande Prairie country and the adjoining prairie areas of the Upper Peace river, as distinguished from the Vermilion settlement, which is on what we call the Lower Peace river. These widely separated districts differ both in latitude and in altitude, the Vermilion settlement being at a lower altitude and a higher latitude than the Grande Prairie settlement, which occupies a position comparatively near the foot of the mountains, and is at a fairly high altitude. I do not suggest that the station at Beaverlod'ge was unwisely placed, but it is desirable that the work be amplified because owing to the possibilities of the country, the large influx of settlement and the differences in latitude and altitude, the results at Vermilion are not conclusive in regard to Grande Prairie, nor is the work at Grande Prairie conclusive in regard to Vermilion. The two sets of experiments are necessary in order to give the full development that is desirable to that great Peace river country.

I am not disputing at all the force of a great deal of what my hon. friend says; in fact, I cordially agree with what he says. What he says in regard, for instance, to the district he has been touching on is practically equally true of all our north country from Quebec right through to British Columbia.

No.
Mr. BURRELL. It is true in certain portions. There is a great deal of immigration, for instance, into British Columbia.

The returns of the Interior Department, which are very conclusive, state that there is no comparison between the quantity of settlement going into the Peace river country and that going into any other equal area in the North country.
Who is in charge of that department?

Some years ago the
Botanical and Entomological branches were simply divisions of the Experimental Farm system, but the entomological work of this country began to develop so much and there were so many important problems that were not directly associated' with the Experimental Farm work that we came to the conclusion we had better establish a separate Entomological Branch, and Dr. Hewitt, who was at the head of the division when it was in the Experimental Farm system, was made its head. He has capable officers under him in almost every province studying out the different problems, establishing field laboratories and working out the histories, not only of injurious pests, but of friendly insects that keep down the predacious ones. For instance, we get from some part of the country reports of some new pest that becomes established which we could not study on the farm and the combatting of which is

of vital interest to farmers over a large section. My hon. friend probably knows about that moth which is now in Nova Scotia and which has cost the eastern United States $6,000,000 within the last twenty or thirty years.
Has the department any report as to the progress made in fighting the ravages of the brown-tail moth in Nova Scotia?

We have pretty lull reports, and I think on the whole we have been able to keep a fairly satisfactory check on it. This is a work of enormous importance and of very great value. We are endeavouring to combat the ravages of this moth in two or three different ways. We are keeping a staff of men travelling all the time through the orchards and fields of the country, destroying its nests and eggs and in two or three different laboratories we are breeding insects which prey on the brown-tail moth both in the moth form and in the larvae form.
What is the line of cleavage between items 44 and 45? What has been done in the county of Middlesex in regard to this branch? Who is the expert and what has he been doing?

The difference between items 44 and 45 is that item 44, the Branch of Entomology, deals with all general questions of insect pests and insect life injurious or beneficial to the farmer, and item 45 deals with those phases of the work which come under the operation of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act. Under that Act, we are dealing with the brown-tail moth, for instance, and with various forms of entomological and botanical work. After practically making it impossible in Europe to grow white pine, this disease of white pine blister rust has been imported into this country and is threatening the existence of our white pine, which is worth about $200,000,000. We are beginning to do a great deal of valuable experimental work to endeavour to combat the work of that disease; that is done under the Destructive Insect and Pest Act. My hon. friend probably alludes to the fact that we established in 1913 one of our field laboratories at Strathroy for the special study of all insects injurious to plant life. We are carrying on work there that will be of benefit to the whole district.
What ha3 the expert there accomplished in connection with that work?
When my Estimates are up again, I shall, I hope, be able to give that information.
What is the expert devoting his attention to in particular?

Reverting again to the question of rust, which comes more properly under this head, although the blame is laid on the barberry bush, the fact remains that that bush is with us all the time, but that rust comes only once in ten or twelve years. Can the Government, through their Director of Experimental Farms, or otherwise, furnish us with any information as to what effect the rust, which was so severe last year, will have on this year's crop? Will this rust remain in the soil causing any trouble, and what will be the effect of sowing seed that has been rusted? Those are questions that the farmers in our country are asking to-day.

Although I am not
thoroughly familiar with this particular fungus, I understand that the rust is not transmitted through the seed. In a lot of these obscure fungus diseases the spores may be lying dormant in the seed, only waiting for favourable climatic conditions to develop. Last year conditions in Manitoba were extremely favourable to the development of this fungus. It is quite true that the barberries that harbour that particular rust are rather a source of danger. Some years ago the Department of Agriculture in Ontario, recognizing the danger, passed legislation for the destruction of all barberries. But the barberry bush, not only the purple kind but others, is a highly ornamental plant, and so many protests were made that the Government made the law operative only with the good will of the municipalities; that is, if .a certain number of people in a municipality wanted the bushes destroyed the law was enforced. The consequence was that the law became a dead letter. In the West conditions are a little different, because there are comparatively few barberries, although I imagine in cities like Brandon, Winnipeg and Moosejaw both forms of the barberry would be hardy enough to live. They are highly ornamental, and a man with a beautiful hedge of them would be sorry to see them destroyed. So far we have hesitated taking any such action, although that may later on be desirable. We are having Mr. Fraser inquire into this question, and if we come to the conclusion that it is in the interests of the farmers to eliminate the barberry entirely from the western country, we shall
have no hesitation in recommending such action.
What about the rust lying dormant for ten or twelve years?

Like all other forms
of disease there might be a certain percentage of rust there all the time, but climatic conditions might be such that it would not develop until the twelfth year.

Could nothing be
used in the ground to kill the rust?
There is a great deal of obscurity about this disease. It may be entirely dormant for several years, only to break out when conditions are favourable.

In 1904, when the rust was not nearly so severe, the next year's crop was hardly affected at all. Has the minister been able to find out whether the failure in the wheat crop last year was entirely due to rust? I do not profess to have any scientific knowledge on this question, but I am strongly of the opinion, and it is also the impression of the farmers in my district, that rust was not the only cause of' last year's failure. We had a very great deal of snow, and a very late spring. We could not get on the ground to sow until unusually late in the year. I think the season had never been s'o late before. Seed that should have been sown on the 1st of May was not sown until the 1st of June. Then came splendid growing weather, plenty of rain and moisture, and lots of warm weather, and the grain grew very quickly. The wheat had never looked better, and every one thought it would run from 40 to 45 bushels to the acre. I never saw longer heads, but when they were shelled only three or four shrivelled kernels would come out. The impression was that the grain grew very quickly, but had very little root. Furthermore, we did not have very many hot winds last year, as we had in other years. Our people do not believe the failure was due entirely to rust, but that there was some other blight on the crop.

My information is that the failure was almost entirely due to rust, and that there was very little blight indeed. Wheat at certain stages of its growth is more immune than at other times from a violent attack of rust, but if the development of the rust fungus happens to coincide with a particular period in the growth of the wheat the grain may be damaged very seriously. My information at present is that last year's failure was due to rust, but I

hope, before another year, to have further information on this fungus.

One of the troubles' in
Ontario, and I suppose in other provinces, is the weed pest; I refer particularly to mustard and daisies. I think there is enough land in Ontario covered with these weeds tp supply wheat for the people of all the province. So long as I can remember, the Ontario Government has been experimenting with methods for killing weeds. When the farmers' organizations held their meetings regularly I attended them all, and I have been told time and again that a certain solution had been discovered which, if applied at a certain time of the year and in a certain way, would kill mustard. But next year the mustard w.ould come up just as thick as ever on the next farm, if not on the one where the solution had been used. Has anybody really jdiscovered a. death blow to these pests? We are talking about increased production these days, and if some way could be discovered of eradicating these weeds, I think on the land thus cleared in Ontario we could grow enough wheat to feed all the people of our province. Surely if the Federal and Provincial Departments of Agriculture took up this question, some way could be found of killing these pests so that they would stay killed with proper care. I am afraid the Ontario Government has not been successful in this direction, although I am told that in some cases their efforts have met with success. But wherever you go in the country to-day you can see these weeds in abundance. Has the Federal Department of Agriculture taken any action along this line, and if so, are their efforts likely to meet with success?

My hon. friend has not, like myself, been engaged in farm work for "a great many years. The weed problem is a very old one, and if my hon. friend thinks we can develop a specific for killing all weeds he is gping to be very much mistaken. It all depends on the personal equa- -tion. A good farmer who knows how to handle his land by rotation of crops, and keeps it in go.od shape, is not going to be very much troubled with weeds. When we first bought the Experimental Farm it was absolutely infested with every kind of weed known to the province.
How is it now?

Pretty good. I have
been in districts in my hon. friend's province and found conditions different. I can

go into one district and find a farm seeded down with bad weeds, and I can go to another district, where the farmer kept his farm in good shape with a rotation of crops, and I will find the farm perfectly clear of weeds. It is the personal equation and the knowledge of how to handle crops that counts.

Is there any solution
which, if applied every season, would kill wild mustard and daisy?
No.
What about 5 pm. dandelions?

They are very bad; they are in the category with daisies; they spread themselves out and kill everything in sight. My hon. friend says it is the personal equation that counts, and of course that is the big factor in everything. Canada is not so infested with the Canadian thistle as with other weeds. They have been experimenting in the provinces with a solution which they say, if applied, will kill these weeds, hut the weeds are still growing. It strikes me that, as a result of our scientific investigation, there should be something found that would kill these weeds. The spraying of fruit trees, done regularly, kills the insects, and consequently the development and the production of fruit is greatly assisted. Is there not something which could be used against the other pests in the same manner? If the Agricultural Department could devise something really effective, they would be doing more fo/r development and production than they have' yet accomplished.

We know that insects on fruit trees can be killed by spraying, but there you are treating animal life which is existing on vegetable life. I do not think the spraying of weeds has been found to be very satisfactory, and I understand they are largely giving it up, because in that case you are dealing with a more persistent and hardier type of vegetable growth than cultivated plants. The weeds have survived through hundreds of years, and it is a case of the survival of the fittest. The mustard seed will retain its germinating powers in the ground longer than any other seed known. There is nothing on earth to kill the mustard and daisy except a systematic course of good farming, rotation of crops, and breaking up of the ground. It is a question of labour and intelligence to clean out the weeds, and I do not think you can

manufacture any specific that will do that work.
I have heard farmers say that placing manure on the land makes matters worse.
Yes, if it is not handled properly; the manure may be full of weeds of the worst kind.
Could the minister give me the name of the farmer in Bonaventure who tried the experiment last year?
E. M. Legallis.
And the results were satisfactory?

It is only the first year, and it would be hard to say. I should like to say a word to the hon. gentleman from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) who asked me about the brown-tail moth, because it is just as well to have one or two facts on record. The work is being done from Fredericton where we have our station, We are doing scouting work in connection with the brown tail moth all through New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and, in spite of the spread of the moth from the United States to these provinces, we think we have it well under control. In New Brunswick we have men employed all winter. Infestation exists in the counties of Carleton, York, Sunbury, Queens, Kings, and Charlotte. In Nova Scotia five counties: Hants, Kings, Annapolis, Digby, Yarmouth and Shelburne, are all more or less infested, and the southern part of Quebec is being scouted for the brown tail moth, though no infestation has been found. Through the courtesy of the United States Department of Agriculture who have been importing parasites of the gipsy and brown tail moth from Europe and Asia, and we have continued the breeding of parasites of one of the predaceous beetles. We have colonies of these insects established in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec. Since the work began four years ago, we have reared, collected and imported into Canada over 100,000 insect enemies of the brown tail and gipsy moth. The gipsy moth has not yet reached Canada. It is forty or fifty miles south of the line, but by importing and breeding these parasites which live on the gipsy moth, we hope to have a valuable ally in preventing it being established in the country at all.

How is the scout system
carried on?

We have been co-operating with the provinces. The provinces have given a certain amount of men and we have given a certain amount of men. Year after year we have had men who have been very active and energetic doing this work, and we thought it better to continue the same men, in preference to having new men, who would have to be taught each year.
What has been done to protect against rust in the West? In a word, has the minister made any progress in the way of giving out information, so that farmers may get rid of the rust in their wheat?

As a matter of fact, we have only started to work. We have established two laboratories, one at Brandon and one at Indian Head, and engaged the services of the very best man on the continent, Mr. W. P. Fraser, formerly of Macdonald College, has gone to take charge of that work and carry on the investigation. He will work out every phase of the life history of the. rust, and the best means to combat its ravages. We have also issued about a hundred thousand copies of a poster which gives an absolutely life-like illustration of the rust in all its forms, with directions and suggestions so far as we are familiar with the matter at the present time. Our actual investigation work has not gone very far, because Mr. Fraser .only went out there lately. We hope to have a good deal of valuable work done in the course of a year.

Could you make any
recommendation as to one class of wheat seed less liable to be attacked by rust than another?

I have been informed that they have been giving a good deal of attention to that in the States, but, so far, they have not been able to come to any conclusion as to one particular variety more free from it than another.
Was it not the case that last year Marquis wheat was freer in the ratio of one to ten from rust than Red Fife?
No, not any freer than the other.
Oh, yes.
From rust?
From rust. I would say that there would he ten fields of Red Fife rusted to one of Marquis last year.

It may be possible that the reason is, as I explained to my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Sehaffner), that rust will attack wheat at a particular stage of its growth more especially if the rust fungus is also at the proper stage. These two conditions being present, the attack is very much more vigorous. The Marquis wheat may develop at a different time in a particular district and the rust may develop later and in this way the wheat might escape attack. But, speaking generally, through the western country there has not been this difference which my hon. friend suggests.
It does not necessarily follow that Marquis comes in the dangerous season as it is earlier than Red Fife.
That is probably true but any grain that is sown earlier and that develops earlier will probably have a greater tendency to escape owing to the greater vigour of the plant.
If the department has knowledge that Red Fife is more likely to come in the danger zone in regard to time why not advise the farmers of that?
Everything that is known to the experimental stations has been communicated to the farmers in the circular to which I have referred.
When I asked the minister he stated that there had been no information given to the. people as to the difference between one kind of wheat and the other.
Was there any difference between Red Fife and Marquis in regard to liability to attack from rust?
The difference was about ten to one in favour of Marquis.
In our country I do not think there was any difference between Red Fife and Marquis.
Are the wheat growers in eastern Canada troubled with rust to the same extent as the western wheat growers are?
Very seldom.

More wheat is being grown in eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton than ever before. If there is any way to guard against the attack of rust it would be well to give warning to the wheat growers and any information which the department may have should be communicated to them

with the view of affording protection against that particular pest.

Wheat in the eastern provinces is very seldom attacked. There may be some climatic conditions under which it may occur. Any information we get in the West that is of value to the East will be distributed.

Are not the local experimental farms in Alberta going into this question very fully? There is one at Carlsholme, and there are local branches at other points. Are they not carrying on investigations, and if so, does not this department collaborate with them?

I cannot tell my hon. friend to what extent they are making a special study of this particular rust. We have had some little correspondence with them, but I understand they are practically leaving this special work to us. We have the very best man who can be got on the continent in Mr. Fraser, of Macdonald College. He is acknowledged in the United States to be the best man on this particular class of disease, and we are willing that he should give his whole 'time to the study of this rust.
Apart from this important gentleman who is giving his time to the study of the rust question, who is the chief botanist?
That is under the Director of Experimental Farms.
What are the duties of the chief botanist? What is his name? I have forgotten his name; he is a German.
There is no chief botanist at the present time. The Director of the Experimental Farms is acting as chief botanist.
There is a doctor something-I know the gentleman, but I forget his name.
I suppose my hon. friend is alluding to Mr. Gussow, who was placed in the department by Mr. Fisher about eight years ago.
It is of no importance when he was placed in the department. I was not alluding to who appeinted him, and I do not care.
He is not the chief botanist.
What is his office?
He is acting in the department, but not in the responsible position of chief botanist.
What is his position?

He is carrying on
laboratory work in the laboratory at the Central Experimental Farm.
What is the increased acreage under cultivation in the West this year?

Our information is that there is about eight or ten per cent less wheat under crop throughout the West this year, but that is more than made up by the increased acreage of barley and oats. In Southern Alberta, I understand, there is a little more wheat than last year. The increased acreage throughout Canada will be seven or eight per cent.

There is another variety of wheat I have heard spoken of as being exceptionally early-Prelude. Is any experimentation going on in connection with that wheat with a view of finding out whether it would escape rust or not?

I do not know that we can say anything as to its exemption from rust. We are carrying on some work in regard to Prelude, and the director tells me that we are carrying on a lot of work in our northern stations. The wheat that my hon. friend speaks of is very much earlier than Marquis. It gives very good results at Fort Vermilion, in'the Peace River country.

I would like to revert for a moment to item 43, as I was not in the House when it was taken up. I see by the Auditor General's Report that at the farm at Fredericton, which is the only experimental farm in my province, the expenditure for the year ended March 31, 1916, was $42,618.87. I would like to have some information with regard to the crops under cultivation, the yield per acre, and the position and condition of that farm at the present time.

I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend that information in detail, because all these reports are in process of compilation now as to the exact acreage, character of the crops that are grown, and the experiments that have been carried on. I may say though that about 300 acres are under crop now.

Something like $1,966 was received from the sale of stock in the year
131 i
1915-16. That seems to he the only revenue from that farm. With an expenditure of $42,000 on a farm that has been established for some years, we might expect some considerable return to help meet the cost of maintenance. The general expenditure on these farms should be repaid to a certain extent, and quite a large extent, by the proceeds of what is sold.

My hon. friend will find a full statement of the returns from all the farms at page A-91 of the Auditor General's Report. My hon. friend's argument is often made in connection with experimental farm work in all countries, and at first sight it seems reasonable, but it is based on an entire misconception of the whole nature of the work of. experimental farms. What my hon. friend says would be absolutely true of a demonstration or model farm, but no experimental farm on earth ever should pay; if it did pay it would not be an experimental farm. That is a safe proposition. In order to have a farm pay by the selling of animals and crops it would be necessary to devote all of the acreage and all of the labour to the production of articles for sale, but an experimental farm is worth nothing unless it can do what an individual cannot do, owing to the great expense, that is to make thousands of experiments of all kinds to eliminate those that have been shown to be useless after a number of years. But if one experiment is successful it will justify the experiments carried on for many years. Let me take a familiar illustration, that of the Marquis wheat, referred to by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). Untold thousands of dollars were spent by the late Government and the preceding Government in the effort to produce a wheat that would be an improvement on the Red Fife. Thousands of experiments were made with little plots of ground at the farm here, crossing different varieties, and thousands of these were absolutely useless in so far as the value of the resulting variety is con-cemed. But by crossing a Himalayan wheat with the old Red Fife, out of a great many hybrids produced, one was so promising that it was replanted and tried next year at all the stations. After a few years the type became so fixed and its advantages so apparent that it was given a name, Marquis, and put into general use, its great advantage being that it ripened ten days earlier than the old Red Fife. That quality has made it of incalc alable value; I venture to say that the originating of that variety has paid many times over

for all the cost of all the experimental farms since the first establishment of a farm in 1887. There have been thousands of experiments in grains that were not of such great value. What is true of grain is true of cattle and plants and all kinds of fruit. So I repeat that no experimental farm can ever pay or should ever be expected to pay, and that the return from the sale of crops is a bagatelle, and must be, in comparison with the cost of administration.

My hon. friend seemed to
take it for granted that I was arguing against experimental farms.
No, hut I thought you laid undue stress on that feathre.
I did not intend to do that. Would the minister give us some information as to the manner in which the results .of the work at the farms are disseminated .among the farmers?

That information is distributed by bulletins; circulars and reports, and successful results at one farm are incorporated in further research work at all the farms. Then our men from each farm visit the other farms and bring back information to those in their district. That is in addition to the visiting of the farms by farmers to see what is being done.
I understand that the farmers get no information from these experimental farms.
I am informed that several thousand people from different parts of the province visited the Experimental farm at Fredericton last year.

I think my hon. friend has been misinformed. A farmer's picnic is held there occasionally, which is attended by about a score of people. The Experimental Farm is, no doubt, doing splendid work in the way of getting information for those who are running the farm and for those who live nearby, but complaint is made that the information is not spread among the farmers throughout the province as it should be.

We have the names of a good many thousand New Brunswick farmers on our mailing list. The farm at Fredericton is comparatively new, and there has not been time to develop the experimental work which may be expected within the next- five or six years. We shall gladly add to our list any names that are sent in; my hon. friend is right in saying that the " TMr. Burrell.!
people should have any information that is of value to them.
I would suggest that my hon. friend get a list of the members of agricultural societies throughout the province and use that as an addition to his mailing list.
We have already done that.

We have on the prairie a very destructive weed known as wild oats. Does the department issue bulletins containing plain talk to plain men as to how to get rid of that weed? The only method that I know of is too expensive for the average farmer.

As far as I know, we have no special bulletin dealing with that particular weed. A very excellent book, however, was issued many years ago on the subject of weeds, of which a larger edition is now available. This book probably deals with all destructive and injurious weeds, and sets forth the best methods of treatment.

Will the minister, the next time he comes with his estimates, bring with him such a publication or circular, or an extract therefrom, dealing with wild oats? It is absolutely impossible to get rid of this weed by the ordinary summer fallowing.
I will bring a copy tonight.

Can the minister give
us any information as to what success attended the establishment of the parcel post system in the way of encouraging the shipment of agricultural products? In the United States, poultry, butter and many other farm products are regularly carried by mail, the United States Department of Agriculture taking a great interest in the matter. I know that the development of the parcel post system is expected to enable people to ship various products of the kind mentioned by my hon. friend. I think, however, that my hon. friend would secure fuller information by bringing, the matter up when the Post Office Estimates are under consideration. use of in the carrying of agricultural products.

a special intere i in that work, and I am surprised that my hon. friend cannot give us the information.
