When the parcel post system was authorized by Parliament it was anticipated that a great benefit to the farming community would result, and that the consumer and the producer would he brought closer together. Unfortunately, the Postmaster General is engaged with matters connected with recruiting and is not here to give us the information. Can the hon. minister not tell us whether the farmers are availing themselves of the parcel post for the shipment of their products? Does not the minister think he should give us this information, which, I am sure, would be received by every one with great interest.

I am most happy to
convey to the House any information that I can secure, but I frankly confess I do not know to what extent farmers throughout the country have availed themselves of the parcel post system for the shipment of their product's. After all, many of these matters have been dealt with by the different provincial legislatures, and until recently absolutely nothing was done in the Department of Agriculture in regard to marketing. It is only within the last two or three years that we have begun to pay any attention to the larger marketing possibilities such as livestock, and we have created a market for that purpose. During the regime of my hon. friend no attention was paid to such matters and he cannot expect me already to have such a mass of information that I can give in detail what every market gardener or farmer throughout the country is doing.

I do not expect the minister tp give the House information as to what all the farmers throughout the country are doing, neither do I expect that the country will accept as a good answer to the question as to what this Government is doing, the statement that the old Government neglected its duties tp the farmers.

I am simply pointing
that out.

This country is advancing and we expect a progressive Government to do its full duty, even although the former Government was not just as progressive as it might have been. I do not know whether it was or not, but it did the best it could. Yve are, however, getting new ideas these days, and we have to-day an example in the neighbouring republic of the wonderful development which has taken place in connection with the parcel post system. Why should that not take place in this country? It is a matter of great surprise to me that the minister should say:	I have had this important
work going ,on for only two or three years, and I am not able to tell the House and the country what are the results that have flowed from it. The minister says that if he can get the information, he will do so. That is very laudable. When will the minister give us the information?
iMr. BURRELL: My hon. friend, knows perfectly well that he cannot pin me down to giving an exact date. I am very sprry that my hon. friend is so deeply pained over this matter. I can only tell him what I told him before, that I will have my officials look into the matter, and whatever we can do in the way of getting information or assisting in .this matter will he very gladly done. Unfortunately, in view of all the nice things my hon. friend has said, this Government is not perfect. Rome was not built in a day,

If there is in the world one thing in regard .to which I can agree \ :th my hon. friend, it is that this Govern-n, nt is not perfect. That statement will meet with full approval .throughout the country. Even if this Government is not perfect, will the minister promise, that if we do not detain him to-night, before this session is over, he will place before Parliament a statement made by himself in conjunction with the Postmaster General or the acting Postmaster General of what has been the results of the inauguration of the parcel post system in the way of bringing about and encouraging that close intimacy of contact between the farmer as the producer and the city-man as the consumer that will enable the. one to get a more ready market for perishable products and the other to receive those products upon reasonable and fair terms? As I have said, the Department of Agriculture in the United States has taken charge of the matter there in conjunction with the Post Office Depart-

With all deference to the gentleman to whom my hon. friend from West Peterborough refers, I do not see how that should be. If it be the case, of course, we ought to know it, because that was one of the great advantages held out to the people of this country in connection with the expenditure that would necessarily be incurred in establishing the parcel post system. I would not for a moment think of doing any injustice to the minister.
If anybody ventures to ask the minister a question, or to criticise him, he thinks some injustice is being done. Why, we are here for the very purpose of criticising matters in respect of which we think objection should be made. I am quite disposed to recognize all that the department has done, but I think that very much more might be done along the lines which have been suggested.	-

As I may foe said to foe the father of rural mail delivery in Canada,
I might, perhaps, say that when it was introduced in this country, in 1908, we followed the example of the United States Post Office Department, and if my hon. friend from Peterborough will read their reports as to the object and results of the parcel post and rural mail delivery he will find that the service was established in the United States on a cheap popular basis, primarily for the benefit of the farmers. The Hon. Mr. Wilson, who was formerly Minister of Agriculture in the United States, was in office at that time and he published a report on parcel post and rural mail which I commend to my hon. friend, and in which he states that by the establishment of rural mail delivery the farmer has been brought nearer to the large centres, and that real parcel post, not the sham we have in this country, will solve the problem of distribution of farm products. During my tenure of office as Postmaster General parcel post was not on the raw basis which has since Obtained in this country; it was then only in the experimental stage.
I do not begrudge the extension of the service that has taken place, although I am afraid it has increased the expenditure of the department to a very great extent. I do not begrudge it, however, because it is in the interest of the farmers that they should be brought nearer to the urban centres and should haye the advantage of getting the newspapers and agricultural papers and the many bulletins on farm work which are distributed amongst the farmers here, I suppose, just as is done in the United States.
What about the daily market reports?

The market reports are published in the daily papers, in just the same way as fishing intelligence is sent all over the country. Although the expenditure on rural mail delivery has increased to a remarkable extent, I am in favour of that channel through which to reach the farmers as I believe it is in their interests. Mr. Wilson used that channel in the United States, and I think he was the propelling influence in establishing rural mail and cheap parcel post in that country.
We all remember the discussion which took place in this House some years ago in regard to parcel post. I then ventured to predict that the tentative attempt made by the then Postmaster General, Hon. Mr. Pelletier, would be absolutely futile, and so it has proved. Although several officers
have been appointed in the several cities of the Dominion to look after parcel post, parcel post as they have it in the United States really does not exist in this country. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has always been courteous with members of this House, and has always been ready to take into consideration any suggestion a member might make in the interests of the farmer, and I think this is a question which he ought to tackle with the Post Office Department and with the Government generally. Give the farmers of this country cheap parcel post, and you will have practically solved the problem of distribution.
Where parcel post for eggs and other perishable produce fell down was with the consignee. Who is going to guarantee payment by the consignee?

If my hon. friend will read the reports of the United States Post Office Department, if not the last one the one immediately preceding, he will see that the system has worked very satisfactorily there, and is earning large profits for the Post Office Department.

For the development of the dairying industries and the improvement in transportation, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products, $155,000.

I promised the hon.
member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross) to refer to the work being carried on at Strathroy, and I shall put the information on Hansard. The statement of the work is as follows :
Entomological Laboratory at Strathroy, Ont.
The chief work carried on at this laboratory is a thorough study of white grubs and their control. These insects feed on the roots of grasses, destroying permanent pasture, corn, etc., and are also very destructive to potatoes. Strathroy was selected prime ly on account of the large acreages of corn and potatoes grown in that region. This investigation on white grubs is being carried on in co-operation with the Bureau of Entomology of the United States Department of Agriculture with a view to covering the whole area in which damage from white grubs occurs, thereby obtaining the fullest possible information. In Canada we are investigating these insects at Ottawa, Strathroy, Ont., and Treesbank, Man. Alreauy facts have been secured which enable us to advise farmers as to the best rotations to use and cultural operations to avoid injury from white grubs in districts where they occur. The
Have you any record as to whether the production of cheese this year is low or high as compared with last year?

It is very similar. There was an enormous production last year on account of the Very favourable conditions [DOT] for our dairying, and at the present time conditions are just 'as favourable. There are certain difficulties in regard to labour, but we are looking forward to a very big production.
Towards the encouragement of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of perishable food products, $50,000.
I observe a decrease in the vote, which would seem to indicate that not as many may ,ake advantage of tihe aid as last year.

The reason is that in the initiation of the system the cost was very great. In the last few years many of the heavier payments have been falling off, and there have not been as many cold storages established, because the territory has been pretty well covered. Speaking from memory, we have only established three or four during the last four or five years, and in some of these cases, where the expenditure was very heavy, they have almost entirely completed their payments.

Under this heading, it
would not he inappropriate to ask the Min-
ister of Railways whether the Government, in view of the discussion which has taken place, and in view of the admitted increasing very high cost of living, has given serious attention to the suggestion that the Government take over the cold storage enterprises of; Canada, and operate them for the public good at the least possible cost. Even while we were discussing it the other night, the price of bread went up one cent a loaf, notwithstanding all the promises made by the Minister of Labour.

But it went down again. My hon. friend realizes, as well as I do, what an enormous proposition that would be to consider very seripusly, because the cold storages scattered all over the country, apart from those assisted by the Government, represent a vast amount of money, and it would be very difficult for the Government tp operate them. We are getting a lot of information in regard to the matter, and that has been done very largely under the Order in Council passed recently and which is being administered by the Minister of Labour. The Government is investigating the whole subject much more thoroughly than ever before, but I dpubt whether it would be advisable to take over the whole cold storage system.

It seems to me, as the Government is seriously considering the nationalization of the railways that it would be far easier at the present time to nationalize the cold storage system of Canada. I think the high cost of living has reached such a mark that the people are expecting the Government to do something in this line. What are the regulations at present governing those cold storages at Montreal, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, and other large centres? Is there any authority on the part of the Government tp release some of the food after a certain time, or can the owner of the cold storage establishment keep those products for what length of time he chooses? Really, the time has come when the Government should consider the question whether the food should not be released from cold storage. A charge is made against the cold storage-I do not say it is true-but the time has come when the Government should consider whether or not the cold storage plants should not be nationalized. Food has reached such a price that people cannot live in a reasonable way. It is impossible for a man who has a fixed income of, say, $1,000 or $1,200, and who has a family of three or four children, to live and provide for his family. This is a very

serious question, and I would like my hon. friend to tell the committee whether the Government really intend to do something in the matter. I am not revolutionary, I am not socialistic, I do not wish to grab any other man's property, but in view of the crisis through which we are passing, is it not time for the Government to seriously consider the propriety of nationalizing the cold storage system so that food may be released for the consumers at a reasonable figure?	.

The question which my hon. friend has raised is a very big one indeed. Even if, as he suggests, food in the cold storages were released, it does not follow that the conditions to which he has referred would be in any way relieved. If you were to take out the relatively small amount of food in the cold storages all over the country to-day, it would keep the population going but a very short time. A comparatively small amount of the food that is used is put in cold storage, and if the cold storages were actually abolished it is questionable whether food would be cheaper. I cannot believe that it would be very much cheaper. This is a very intricate question. We are to be provided with full information on this question, and that information will be laid before the House. But, in the meantime, I may say that taking over all the cold storages is almost like taking over a commercial line of business which involves going into every city and town of this country and practically conducting a business operation which would involve the Government in endless difficulties, and, in a sense, would involve it in more difficulties than the nationalization of the railways. You are taking hold of an ordinary business concern, dealing with the question of supply and demand with regard to all conceivable kinds of products, buying and selling, and I think my hon. friend, if he were to look into some of the difficulties surrounding that proposition, would realize that it is a very big one indeed. I am quite aware that the cost of living has gone up to a point where it is pressing on a great many people, and pressing very hard, and I need not assure my hon. friend that the Government, as well as every thoughtful individual in this country, is giving the whole matter an immense amount of consideration. But the difficulties are not such as this or any other Government can solve very readily. I am fairly familiar with what has been done in Great Britain and, to some extent, in France, Italy, and
even Germany, with reference to the question of food control, but the difficulty has been so great that even where they had taken action they have had actually to reverse the action that they had taken. They have found immense difficulties. They are finding them in the United States. They are taking great powers but they admit that it will be very difficult to exercise those powers. The real reason is not that which has be

 ''i'"''ed upon by my hon. friend so much as the absolute world shortage of food supplies. In the present condition of Canada, as wed as of the United States, the cost of the production to the farmers, owing to the tremendous shortage of labour, has been contemporaneous with the mounting cost of food supplies. The increased cost of production and the diminished amount of the product are to my mind almost entirely responsible for the increased cost of food and the increase is general. In every country in tne world, the cost is the indicator really of the world's resources, and although it is true that here and there the speculative element may enter into the question of cost, yet, on the whole the mounting cost is an indication of the shortage that exists in every particular commodity. I [DOT] am quite sure that throughout the world, and in Canada as well, that condition that my hon. friend alludes to is more directly traceable to the shortage of supplies and to the decrease in production than to any other cause. However, I can assure my hon. friend that we are giving consideration to this question.

I have here the index table showing the increase in the cost of' living for the average family. According to the statistics gathered by the Department of Labour in sixty cities in Canada, in April, 1914, the cost for the average family was $7.51 per week. That is very low. In April of this year the cost had risen to $10.77 per week and, with the addition of coal, wood, lighting and rent, the total is brought up to $17.34. I have a list of the prices of various commodities. It is simply appalling and I do not know what the people can do to maintain themselves and to be cheerful under these circumstances. I do not wish to make any appeal that would savour of demagoguery, but' I must say that it is a serious situation. The Government and Parliament are about to consider the nationalization of railways, and that is a very important question that demands an early solution, but is it not a fact that the question of food and the nationalization of cold storage is far more im-[DOT] portant than the nationalization of rail-

ways? You will have riots in this country next winter, you will have bread riots, if the Government do not take a firm hand now to control food. I was also referring a moment or two ago to rentals and the price of coal. I wish to give this warning. About ten days ago I was in New York attending a meeting as a director of a railway company which has subsidiary lines in Canada. The president of the Delaware and Hudson Railway Company, which takes care of most of the coal transportation from Pennsylvania to Canada, said to me: "I am amazed, Mr. Lemieux, to find that at this date we have not half of the coal transportation to Canada that we had last year or the year previous. What are you thinking about in Canada? You will suffer next winter if you have not your coal." But that is aside from the question. I simply wished to refer to_that conversation to show that if the Government do not take with a firm hand the control and transportation of fuel and the control of food, they will have a very serious situation to contend with in Canada. It is the duty of the Government to see to it that such conditions do not arise. I am very sincere. The Government should take hold now of the cold storage situation and, if need be, make terms with the companies that are controlling the cold storage establishments; otherwise you will have riots in this country. I hope they will not occur hut if the cost of living increases a few notches more, you will remember what I said this evening in the House. I do not wish that to happen, and I hope the Government will be patriotic and firm enough to boldly take this question in hand and settle it according to the best interests of the people.

Would the minister give us some information about the exportation of food and especially of farm products to the United States and other countries? Has any action 'been taken by the Government? I am informed that along the north shore of the St. Lawrence river for the past few days dealers from Maine and Vermont have 'been going to the farmers and inducing them to sign contracts at a stipulated price for all their products for the coming year, eggs, fowl, sheep and cattle. I appreciate the difficulty of controlling such a situation, but I should like to know if the minister is informed of the facts and if any steps have been taken or are contemplated.

I have not heard of this matter. [DOT] There is nothing under our present system which would prevent American

dealers purchasing in Canada under such conditions, and making contracts with any farmers who wished to enter into them. I had not heard of the circumstances, but I shall make inquiries.

In the section from which I come there seems to be a very strong feeling that the Government should take some action to regulate the cold storage systems o'f this country, and I join with the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) in saying that the Government should not hesitate a moment to see that storing of food supplies in the different cold storage systems of Canada is regulated in some way. If the cold storage plants are allowed to continue to purchase at the present prices and to fill up their plants it simply means that the prices the consumers will pay next winter will be exorbitant, and the prediction of the hon. gentleman that there will be riots will be fulfilled. I feel satisfied that the Government do not wish that to occur. I had it drawn to my attention the other day, notwithstanding the statement made by the Minister of Labour, that in the different cold storage systems mentioned to me there are $4,500,000 worth of goods. The plants named to me were the Lindsay cold storage, Flavelle Bros, of Peterborough, the Harrison and Kincardine cold storage plants and the Harris Abattoir of Toronto, a subsidiary company to the William Davies Company. If that is true, and I feel satisfied it is, it is sufficiently important for this Committee of this House to investigate before we proceed to pass more money for this purpose. If there is to-day in the cold storage systems I have mentioned over four and one-half million dollars worth of foodstuffs, what will it mean next fall? It means that, with the price that is now being paid to the producer for eggs, forty cents at the farmer's door, the price will be at least double that to the consumer next winter. Eggs are only one commodity. There are other necessities of life concerned, and I feel that we would be justified in asking to have this item stand until the officers of the department investigate the statement I have made. I feel that the Department of Agriculture and the minister himself must feel that there is something radically wrong with the cold storage systems of this country when they are reducing the estimate by over $100,000. If the estimate is to be reduced by "over $100,000 it must mean that the department are not in sympathy with the methods being adopted by the different systems, and this is a further reason why

we should ascertain whether the statements that have been made are correct or not. If they are correct, then it is up to this Parliament to take some drastic action and see that the consumers of this country are not held up as they are reported to be. There seems to be some foundation for the different resolutions that are being passed by consumers, by the labouring men and the people generally, throughout Canada. They feel suspicious that there is something radically wrong, and if such is the case, I believe that we would be doing only our duty in asking to have this item stand pending further investigation.

This question of food supplies and the cost of living is one that seems to be continually with us, but I think it is about time that the members of this House and many of the -people of the country should begin to take a sane view as to the causes of the high cost of living and of the supply of food. I might say that if the proposition of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) should be seriously considered by the Government, they would find many of the cold storage men in Canada delighted with the prospect pf having their cold storage plants taken over, because to-day many of them, and I speak now not of the larger ones of which I know nothing, but many of the medium and small cold storage plants, present a prospect of being white elephants on the hands of the owners.' I can tell the minister that there is a cold storage plant in my riding, one of the very best in western Ontario, that he can take over any day at his own valuation-and the owners will be delighted to get rid of it. We talk pf the high cost of living, but it seems to me that the old Adam remains in us yet, that we are not willing to take the blame that should lie upon ourselves, but want to cast that blame on this person pr that person, or any person who will not resent it. Some people blame it on the farmer; when they have no other person to blame the ppor farmer is attacked. I want to say to-night that the farmer is producing dairy food supplies to-day at a cost of about 75 per cent more than three or four years ago, and if the price has increased, surely the farmer is entitled to at least the increased cost of production. Then there are efforts, such as we have had here to-night and as we have had many times this session, to lay the blame on the cold storage people. The hpn, member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) has just given us a statement which he says he
has received that there are $4,500,000 worth of food supplies in the cold storage plants of this country at the present time.
That was in five which I mentioned.	,

Then take the plants to
which he refers. I regret that there aTe not $25,000,000 worth of food supplies in these plants at the present time. And why do I say that? The fact that there is only $4,500,000 worth of goods in these plants clearly indicates the alarming shortage of meats and dairy produce. $4,500,000 worth of goods would mean 10,000,000 dozen eggs, having regard, to the present prices. How long would 10,000,000 dozen eggs last the people of Canada? I venture to say that if no more goods were placed in these cold storage plants during the period of a month, they would be empty at the end of that time. Undoubtedly prices next fall will be higher than they are to-day, not because the cold storage plants are hoarding food products for higher prices, but because they are unable to get them in sufficient quantities for an ample storage to provide for the shortage which must inevitably come next fall and winter. The farmers of western Ontario to-day get 40 cents a dozen for eggs, whereas they got only 30 cents at the same time last year. In fact, the cold stor-. age men are indifferent as to whether or not they put eggs into cold storage. They are unable to export their eggs as they did to some extent last year, because they cannot get any guarantee of transportation across the Atlantic. For several reasons they are afraid to store goods under present high prices, because they know not wihat may happen before next fall which may subject them to great loss. They are paying considerably more for butter also than they did this time last year. I see nothing in store for us, therefore, except very much higher prices for dairy produce next winter than prevailed last winter.
Hon. gentlemen talk as if cold storage, particularly as relating to eggs, were a new system. As far back as I can remember, and long before that, eggs were preserved in the summer, when they were cheap, for use in winter, when they were expensive. Many hon. gentlemen will remember the old-fashioned method of pickling eggs and putting them in vats; thousands of dozens of eggs were preserved in that way. The preservation of eggs, therefore, did not originate with the cold storage plant; it is simply the method of preservation that has changed.

The remedy for the high cost of living rests not with the Government, although possibly the Government can do something. It rests not with the cold storage people, although possibly they can do a little, too. Nor does it rest with the working man, nor with the man of moderate means, who, after all, is the only man who during the last eight or ten years has been practising economy. The people of the other classes have been living most extravagantly; we are to-day living most extravagantly. An American authority on this subject recently said that there is no reason why every family, excluding, of course, the classes which I have mentioned, should not be able to reduce the cost of their foodstuffs by at least 50 per cent, and at the same time nourish their bodies just as w.ell. Look in our restaurants, our hotels-yes, in our homes-and see the waste of food that takes place from time to time. There is an opportunity of saving foodstuffs; there is a means by which we can reduce the cost, because as the supply increases, prices are reduced. The most effective way of reducing the cost of living and of increasing the supply of foodstuffs is by avoiding waste and extravagance. But the selfish spirit naturally asserts itself. We would rather criticise the Government or the cold storage people than practise self-denial and disappoint our appetites and desires. Individual cold storage concerns may be deserving of criticism, but instead of criticising them as a class, we ought to encourage them. I would almost go so far as to say that the Government ought to give them a little assistance in their efforts to provide against the scarcity of food which must ensue during next fall and winter.
The committee must have been struck by the solution which our two hon. friends have offered to the problem of the high cost of living, namely: Do not eat so much.
Do not w>aste so much.

To my hon. friend from
South Perth I would say that if he feels

he is too extravagant in his expenditure, that is his affair, and I should he glad if he would speak for himself 'and not include me in his suggestion, because I have no guilty feeling along that line at all. I do feel, however, that I pay more for what I get than I ever did before, but I do not admit that I am getting more than I ever did before or more than I am entitled to. I do not suppose that the principle of cold storage as an economic proposition needs any defence at the hands of anybody. No one is attacking the economic propriety of the cold storage system. Neither is anybody suggesting that the_ farmer should not receive as high a price as he can get for his products. If I correctly gathered the sense of the suggestions of my hon. friend from Rouville and my hon. friend from Kent it is not to the fanners' prices or to the use of cold storage that exception is taken, hut the question is raised 9 p.m. as to the manipulation of prices by or for the benefit of those who control the cold storage plants. That is the question at issue in the high cost of living that is interesting to members of Parliament and to the country, and to which they desire to call the attention of the Government. If the consumer only pays what the producer got, plus charges for carrying and other services rendered, nobody has any fault to find; but if the consumer pays what the producer received plus charges for carrying and other services rendered, and also an exorbitant profit, the result of the manipulation of the market, then there is cause for complaint, and we desire to draw the attention of the Government to the possibility of the existence of that condition, and demand correction of it at their hands.
We have had a sufficiently startling instance of manipulation of food prices during the last few months with regard to western wheat. It has already been stated to the House that the wheat left the farmer's hands at a price of from $1.20 to $1.80 per bushel, but the consumer 'has to pay for that flour on the basis of $3 a bushel or over. The farmer does * not get that price, but the consumer pays it. Service was not rendered for that difference in price; it is simply a matter of manipulation resulting in financial benefit to those who are in a position to control the supply of wheat. What has occurred so markedly in the case of wheat is, we believe, occurring every day with regard to those foods which are the subject of cold storage. We believe that the opportunities that necessarily come to those who control cold storage operations, 
not necessarily the owners of the plants, are taken advantage of by those in control of cold storage operations, in the manipulation of prices for their own benefit and to the cost of the consumer. There are many questions facing the people of this country at the present time. I think everybody will admit that to the city dweller at any rate the high cost of living is one of the . most pressing problems he has to face. That being the case, it is the business of the Government of this country to take such measures as can be taken for the purpose of securing an amelioration of that condition. Now, if it is the fact that five cold storage plants in the province of Ontario handle the amount of food that they are said to handle per month, it must be quite obvious that practically the whole food supply passes through these plants and is subject to manipulation at the hands of those in control of the plants.
Do I infer that my hon. friend thinks the people of this country make use of only $4,500,000 worth of such goods per month?

What I say is that $4,500,000 of such goods per month is a very important part of the food supply of that section of the country where those plants are operating, and I am satisfied that the operation of those plants in large measure fixes the price of food to the people of that part of the country, just exactly as the manipulation of wheat last spring fixed the price that my hon. friend has to pay for the flour he buys to-day. It 'being an admitted fact that such a large proportion of the food supply passes through those plants and is therefore possibly subject to undue manipulation for the benefit of those who control these operations, these plants being under the responsibility ,of this Government, and many of them, I believe, receiving aid in actual money from the treasury of this country, it is the paramount duty of the Government, and I would say even before this item passes, to satisfy this House and the country whether or not there is such manipulation of prices of the food products going through these cold storage plants. This question of the high cost of living is with us; it is here now; it is pressing, and it will become more pressing from day to day. If there is an actual scarcity of fo.od in the country then that scarcity makes the food supply still more and more susceptible to manipulation for the profit of those who hold and cpntrol it, and therefore makes it still more necessary that there should be an investigation of the facts of the case.

My hon. friend from Middlesex said that if it should he the case that food is unduly withheld from the market for the purpose of enhancing the price, that would be an abuse. Surely it would be an abuse, and it is an abuse that is known to have occurred in the past, when the conditions of stress that prevail to-day did not obtain. We ask that in the conditions of stress that exist to-day this country be given the guarantee fit the Government that such a condition does not now exist-a guarantee that there is no holding up of the food supply of the people for the purpose of unduly enhancing the price, either by causing undue waste or simply by h.olding back the supply, thereby causing the people who eat three times a day to pay more for the food they eat. I urge upon the minister that he appreciate the importance of this question to the people, and that under the authority that is vested in him-and it is vested in him by the act pf this House-he take measures to satisfy the House and the country that there is no undue manipulation of the food supply under pretense of_ giving it the economic advantage of cold storage.

In answer to the question asked by my hon. friend from Edmonton, the Order in Council to which reference has been made, was passed on the 10th November. We at once proceeded to get ready to make the inquiries authorized by that Order in Council, and the work of sending out questions was begun in the latter part of December. Last night or the night before I gave the House samples ,of the questions sent out to the different wholesale and retail men and manufacturers. We first took up anthracite coal, which appeared to be a more pressing matter than any other. That was followed

by questions in regard to sugar. We asked questions Tuning back for four years, as to the quantities ,on hand at a particular date, the cost, the amount of sales during that year, and we required them to send us a monthly statement as to the quantities on hand, what it cost them, the quantities sold and the prices at which these quantities were sold. For instance, we sent out 300 questions to the leading dealers in anthracite coal throughout the country. We got returns from them under very searching forms of oath. Sometimes these returns were not very satisfactory, and we required further and better answers to the questions. AfteT correspondence, we received what we believed to be satisfactory and truthful returns. We are getting monthly returns now of the quantity of coal each man has on hand at the beginning of the month, what it cost him, how much he bought during the month, and what he is selling it at. I went into details in regard to sugar the night before last. We came to the conclusion that the profits on sugar, for instance, were not unreasonable, averaging generally about fifty cents a ton to the retailer. We got the price of coal at the pit's m.outh, the freight on it, the cost of delivery, the cost of overhead Charges, and so on, and checked the answers we got from each individual by information we had at our disposal from other sources. It is well known that the chief element governing the price of sugar is the cost of the raw material, which has gone up in price 100 per cent since the beginning of the war. The freight on sugar from Cuba has risen from nine cents to seventy-six cents a hundred pounds. The coal used in connection with the refineries has doubled in price. The chemicals that they use in refining sugar have gone up 300 per cent. Bags and packages have gone up in price. Labour has materially increased since the beginning of the year. Two of the refineries in Canada made no profit at all. One was operated at an actual loss. Another made only sufficient to pay interest on the bonds. On the whole, their profits amounted, on the average, to about a fifth of a cent a pound on sugar, which would not he regarded as a very great profit. The last price fixed for sugar was $8.35 a hundred to the wholesaler. Sugar is being sold by the retailer in a great many cases at 9 cents and in some cases, at 10 cents a p.ound, the man having paid $8.35 per hundred for it.
As to cold storage, we have gone into that question very thoroughly. The hon.' member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) a few [Mr. Grothers. 1
nights ago, made a statement in the House that a certain company, perhaps the largest in Canada, operating cold storage, was seeking insurance on commodities aggregating in value about $2,000,000. That seemed to be a large sum of money. I am informed by the president of the company that that sta/tement had no foundation in fact, that they are insured every day according to the amount they have in store, and that it varies from day to day. I have a full statement of that company's business. They have three concerns, one in Montreal, one in Toronto and one in Winnipeg, and we have the particulars of all their business, including beef, bacon, pork, cheese, butter, eggs, fish, and some small articles. We have the details, and we have the amount they actually had on hand at the time the statement was made up. The last statement we got was about the first of April, showing the quantity they purchased every month, the amount on hand, the details of the quantities of these different articles purchased and on hand, the prices they paid and the prices at 'which they are selling them. This evidence shows that if they had $2,000,000 worth of commodities on hand, that would be a very small amount for them and would not last them foT half a month.
If they had $3,000,000 of stock on hand it would not be surprising that they should ask for $2,700,000 of insurance, because that amount of insurance would not be out of proportion.
The president of the company informs me that they had never made application for $2,000,000 of insurance at the same time.

The statement was not made that they were asking for that amount from any one company, but that they were placing that amount of insurance on their stock with different companies in proportionate amounts, not one amount.

I am told by the president of the company that it is not so at all, that they have not asked for insurance to that extent at any particular time from any company or any number of companies. They are insured from day to day as the amount in the storage varies, and it would not likely vary to the extent of $2,000,000 in a day. That company is one that, I am told by the president, does a business amounting to ' about $1,000,000 a week. According to our last report their business for a month

amounted to about $3,000,000. We have every month a statement of the amount bought, the quantity in hand and the selling price. They were turning over about $3,000,000 a month at the time of the last statement, and I am told by the president now that they are turning over $4,000,000 a month; so that $2,000,000 worth of stock on hand would be only half of what they required for the next month. They are largely exporters. I laid on the Table today a report from the commissioner who has been devoting his attention to these inquiries. I laid on the Table reports, which will be found very interesting, concerning anthracite coal and refined sugar. The commissioner has in preparation a report touching cold storage, which will cover every cold storage in Canada. Others will have reference to the canners, flour, ice, bread and potatoes. These reports will follow at no distant date. If hon. gentlemen have time to look over these reports they will find them very interesting. I think they ought to 'be printed and sent out to the people, so that they will see what the exact facts touching cold storage and all these other commodities I have mentioned are. We are satisfied that there is no such thing as withholding in cold storage for the purpose of enhancing prices in the future. Prices are so high now that the keeping in cold storage of a large quantity of these commodities would become useless and would not he warranted. We have a provision in this Order in Council prohibiting the withholding from sale, or accumulation, of any quantity more than a man requires for his own use or for the ordinary purposes of his business. He is bound to sell to the public. Perhaps the committee will 'bear with me while I read again what I read the night before last-clause 3 of this Order in Council. It is in these words:-
. |
No person shall accumulate or shall withhold from sale any necessary of life-
That is defined as including food, fuel and clothing-
-beyond an amount thereof reasonably required for the use or consumption of his household or for the ordinary purposes of his business ;
(2) Every person who shall at any time hold any necessary of life beyond an 5-mount thereof reasonably required as aforesaid, and every -person who shall hold for the purpose of sale, whether as manufacturer, wholesaler, jobber, retailer or otherwise, any stock-in-trade of any necessary of life, shall offer for sale the said excess amount, or the said stock-in-trade, as the case may be, at prices not higher than are reasonable and just.
Has there ever been a conviction under that clause of the Order in Council?

There has been no conviction under it in so far as I am aware, but there is nothing to prevent my hon. friend from West Kent, if he knows of any violation of the section, proceeding with the prosecution of a man for such violation.
I called the minister's attention to a tobacco case and the minister told me to tell the man who was affected to go ahead but refrained from doing.it himself. It is for the Government to do it.

I do not remember receiving any letter from the hon. gentleman concerning tobacco, but I have no doubt it is true if he says so. But tobacco does not come within the provisions of this Order in Council.

Is tobacco not a necessary of life?
v Mr. CROTHERS: It may be but it is not covered by the term "necessaries of life." That term simply covers food, fuel and clothing. My hon. friend (Mr. McCoig) thinks the Government ought to proceed to prosecute. He knows very well that it is not the duty of this' Government to proceed, in so far as criminal, or quasi criminal, laws made by this Parliament are concerned, except where the violation of such laws affects directly the revenues of the country. It is the duty of the provincial governments to enforce the criminal law made by this Parliament. If a farmer in my hon. friend's constituency had one of his horses stolen he would never think of writing down to the Minister of Justice at Ottawa, or to the Minister of Labour, to ask him to prosecute John- Brown for stealing his horse. He would go to the county crown attorney of Kent whose duty it is to look after such matters. If there has been any violation of the- law concerning tobacco, it is up to the local authorities to prosecute. No Government has ever undertaken to prosecute in such cases. Fancy this' Government undertaking to prosecute somebody in Nanaimo, Vancouver Island, for violating the provisions of this Order in Council in regard to milk. As I said a moment ago, that is the provision to prevent withholding. Under section 9, provision is made for prosecuting in a case of that" kind.

section 6, when that Order in Council was



passed, it would have been much better if the Government had named a commission o<r to make inquiry in all Canada as they have done in the United States on entering the war. I shall be glad to
come to my hon. friend's question in a moment. I was about to show the provision of clause 9 which might be applied in case of a violation of clause 3, which I read because the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) raised the question. Clause 9 is in these words:
(1) Any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of these regulations shall be guilty of an Indictable offence and liable upon indictment or upon summary conviction under Part XV of the Criminal Code to a penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years, or to both fine and imprisonment as specified; and any director or officer of any company or corporation who assents to or acquiesces in the contravention or non-observance by such company or corporation of any of the provisions of these regulations shall be guilty personally and cumulatively with hts company or corporation and with his co-directors or associate officers.
There is a provision in this Order in Council that no prosecution shall be held anywhere without the consent of the Attorney General of the province. In case of a violation, of this section 3,1 think it is quite clear, that a man having a cold storage plant would be bound to sell at a reasonable and just price to men to whom he would be selling in the ordinary course of business. I do not think he would be obliged under that clause to sell to a private individual, as he is not a retailer, but I think he would be compellable to sell to a wholesale man at a reasonable and just price, and he would be violating the provision of that clause if he withheld more than was necessary for his own use or for use in the ordinary course of his business. I might call the attention of my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Martin) to a few words in subsection 2 of section 3. One of the officers of the city of Montreal pointed out

the difficulty of proving the excess amount referred to in that clause. The gentleman criticising that clause lost sight altogether of the words "or the said stock in trade." It is not confined to the excess that he would have over and above the amount he would usually have in his possession in the ordinary course of business or for the use of his own family; he is bound to sell not only that excess but the stock in trade, so that if a man in the ordinary course of his business was selling coal and refused to sell a portion of his stock in trade at a reasonable price, he would, I think, be clearly violating that provision of the clause, and with the assent of the Attorney General of the province, the municipality could proceed under section 9 to his prosecution.
Now as to the question raised by my hon. friend from Montreal:	Section 4 of this
Order in Council authorizes the Minister of Labour to make investigations all over the country, not in any one particular place, and section 5 authorizes the municipality to make an inquiry touching matters affecting its own people. While we have not confined our investigations' entirely to such larger questions as affect the whole Dominion, it was thought well to give the municipality power to inquire concerning matters within its own boundaries, and that it would not be practicable for us at Ottawa, for instance, to inquire into a complaint at Nanaimo as to the cost of milk there. And so section 5 was provided in these words :
Whenever the council of any municipality shall declare by way of resolution that In its opinion excessive prices are being demanded within the limits of such municipality for any necessary of life, such council may, by notice in writing under the hand of its clerk or other authorized officer, require any person dealing within the municipality in such necessary of life, and locally situate therein, to make and render unto such council within a time set in such notice, and such person shall make and render unto such council, precisely as required by it, a written return under oath or affirmation, showing in detail-
I need not give the details of the questions they ate thereby authorized to ask and to compel answers under oath. If these answers, come in and are not satisfactory, the municipality, under section b of section 5, may apply to the Minister of Labour to press the investigation further, and further investigation may be made by the Minister of Labour himself or by any one whom he authorizes in writing to take evidence under oath and to require the dealer to produce his books and all that sort of thing under section 6.

But I have notified all the large municipalities in Canada, including the one my hon. friend has the honour to represent, the city of Montreal, that if they comply with section 5 and request me by resolution of the council to authorize one of their officials, the city solicitor or any other official of the municipality, I will authorize him under section 6 to proceed with the fuller examination that I am authorized under that section to make, and any such officer so authorized by me in writing could call witnesses, examine them under oath, compel the dealer to produce his books and investigate the whole matter, and so the officer of the city of Montreal or any other city would have the investigation under his own control. As J said, we have not confined the power of investigation to our own department; we thought it convenient to authorize the municipality to deal with matters within its own boundary. For instance, we have a great many complaints about the cost of milk and bread. Unless we had a staff of officers of about 100 or 200 we could not undertake to inquire into these questions in every city, town and village in Canada. I notified them by circular letter that, as I was authorized under section 6, I would confer that power on any officer of the municipality whom they might name so that they might proceed in these investigations without any further reference to us. It is easy to say that this Government ought to do that sort of thing, but we dp not do it, it is no part of our duty to do it. It is necessary to get the consent of the Attorney General before prosecution can be made, as, for instance, under the Lord's Day Act. No prosecution under that Act can be made without the consent of the Attorney General of the province in which the offence is said to have been committed. So it is under these regulations. The municipal council of a city could not thoroughly investigate the question as to flour. Supposing the council of Montreal appointed some one to ascertain whether the price of flour in Montreal was reasonable or unreasonable, the grocer from whom the flour is bought would say: "I had to pay so much to the miller." Therefore the man in Montreal would have to be acquitted at once, because it would be said that he was simply charging the price which was regulated by circumstances which were beyond his control It seems to me that to effectively carry out any law for the regulating of food prices, and reducing the cost within proper Limits, you must have some authority which has jurisdiction through-

out Canada. The official must have jurisdiction, not only in the place where the finished product is .sold but in the place where lit is manufactured. It seems to me the point raised by the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve that it was the duty of this Government to carry out this law to regulate food prices, and reduce them to proper limits, is one for the Dominion of Canada to deal with, as pertaining to the whole country. Suppose a complaint were made against a man in Halifax by the city council of Halifax, and the dealer says, " It costs me so much for my coal down at the mine in another county." That is 'altogether outside the jurisdiction of the city council of Halifax, and, therefore, if the price charged at the mine were so high that there was not more than a reasonable profit accruing to the dealer in Halifax, the city council would !be powerless. You must investigate [DOT]the whole question. The food controller, or the authority investigating, must look, not only to what has taken place at the point of production, and must consider the nature of the transaction between the wholesaler and retailer. The hon. minister .says this is like the administration of the criminal law. I say it is not, because when Parliament enacts a criminal law, ordinarily nothing further is done. The whole machinery for the administration of that law is left in the hands of provincial authorities, but in this case the Government takes charge of a portion of the machinery, and it appoints people to investigate. It passes an Order in Council and it says to Montreal, " If you will name any-* body, we will appoint him," showing that the Government is taking control of the matter ,or pretending to take control of it, but it is only a pretense To the people of Canada that they are doing something to control food prices, and it is seeking to throw on the municipalities the duty of making an investigation, knowing full well that they have not the machinery to make a thorough investigation, and that, after all, the most that will result from it will be that the Government will be able to make the excuse that they give to the municipalities the power, when they know perfectly well that the duty rests upon the fMr. Pugsley.]
Dominion. Another feature of it is that no criminal proceedings can be taken without the authority of the Attorney General, throwing in the way of , the prosecution another difficulty. What gentleman says " hear, hear?" Is it the hon. gentleman who tried to stop the committee from working?	-

If the hon. gentleman asks me, I would say that I was trying to encourage him to deal with the question before the committee instead of the dreadful condition he pictured in St. John in regard to coal.

The hon. gentleman need not grow impatient. I do not wonder that he wants to get the minister away from this question as quickly as possible, but he will not be able to succeed for a moment at all events. In regard to the cold storage question, the Order in Council is so drawn as really to prevent any effective operation. It does not affect sale to the consumer because the consumer has no Tight to buy from the person having goods in cold storage. The person having goods in cold storage sells to the wholesale dealer or to the retail dealer, but not directly to the consumer. Therefore, no matter what the price may be, the ultimate consumer would not have any complaint under this Order in Council. Who is going to proceed against the cold storage warehouse? It is not the retailer, because the higher the price he pays to the warehouseman the higher the price he charges to his customers. If the retail dealer is complained against under this Order in Council, all he has to say is: " I had to pay so much to the warehouseman, his prices were high and I was entitled to a reasonable profit; therefore, there

can be no complaint against me." The retailer is not likely to enter into litigation with the warehouseman because he desires to keep his relations friendly with the person from whom he buys.
All he has to do is to tack on a little higher price to the consumer to meet the extra price that he is paying to the warehouse man or to the wholesale dealer, and so he suffers nothing. He gets a larger price and a considerably greater profit from the family to whom he ultimately sells the goods. All this shows that it is necessary for the Government to take charge of the whole situation, to thoroughly investigate the prices charged by the warehouse men, the quantity of goods kept in stock, the prices which these goods cost before they were put into the warehouse, and to consider what would be a reasonable charge for the warehouse man, and then, through a food controller, to see that these foods reach the consumer at a reasonable and fair price. I have not time to go more fully into the Order in Council, but I am sure one has only to read it to see that the Order in Council itself and the mode in which the Government propose to enforce it are such as are calculated to render the Order absolutely nugatory and incapable of producing the slightest effect in reducing the cost of food.
The minister says that he sent a telegram to the mayor of Montreal in February. I think it was at the end of March.
Oh, no.
I may be mistaken. And he said that I did not answer it.
I did not say that.
I answered the telegram, but I did not send an attorney to Ottawa.
That is what I said.

Our attorney said to us that we did not need it, we were asking in that telegram for power to make an inquiry and that is what we did the day after. I believe, if my memory serves me well, that a report of that inquiry was sent to the Government. We found that the trouble in respect to coal was not the fault of the small dealer, but the fault of the big dealer in the city of Montreal. I remember very well that last fall the Board of Commissioners and the council of the city of Montreal passed a resolution asking the Government to place

an embargo on the export of different articles such as potatoes. Potatoes last fall cost $2 to $2.75 a bag, and in the spring they cost $4.50 a bag. We made that request but we received no answer. I think that the only thing to do, and I think this is the duty of the Government, is to follow the example of the United States and to name a commissioner to inquire throughout the entire country into the quantity of the different necessaries of life, and to control the price so that nobody will make an undue profit at the expense of the population. That was the duty of the Government, and that is what the Council and Board of Commissioners of the city of Montreal thought last fall. I was answering a letter written to me, I think by the Department of Agriculture, and I suggested in my letter that the only remedy or possible means to give satisfaction and to reduce the cost of living to the citizens of different cities in Canada was to put an embargo on the export of certain foodstuffs. To that letter, which I signed myself, we received no answer. That was the only course which would have given good results. We had an example about a month ago from the President of the United States. It was the duty of this Government to take similar action long ago. Does the Government of the United States control the price of coal in the United States, or has it done anything to control that price?

The first thing they did was to name a commissioner on the cost of foodstuffs. When the time comes to look into the question of the price of coal, they will undoubtedly adopt the same course that they have adopted with regard to the cost of foodstuffs.

I inferred from the hon.
gentleman's remarks that they did control the price of coal, and I asked if that were true.

I am not informed as to that. But the United States having as President such a man as President Wilson, I am sure they will adopt a similar course. But having such people as we have at the head of our Government, they do nothing at all in support of the big city of Montreal in matters of this kind. You are always working on political lines. That is shown by the question you have

put to the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Mo-Coig), asking him if he would (be willing to recommend a maximum price pf $3 a bag for beans. That means that you try to set the farmer against the citizens of the big city in order to make political capital for the next election-it is nothing else. The country should be administered in the interests of all the people, and the Government should not try to make political capital out of such questions as this in order to get back into power. I do not rise frequently in this House, but you know that you have not done your duty towards labour, not alone in the city of Montreal, but in the whole of Canada. Who is the man who most needs an increase of salary if it is not the man who is working 365 days a year-

-and for whom the cost of living is just the same as it is for the man who gets $5,000. But for him you do nothing.

I hope I appreciate the remarks of my hon. friend who has just sat down, and I am not disputing, it is not my place to dispute, the sincerity of his motives in discussing the interests of the large number of people in the city of Montreal over whom he officially presides.
I was speaking for the people throughout the whole of Canada, not in Montreal alpne.

My hon. friend was, of course, speaking more particularly of Montreal. I may say that my conception of the duties of a Government, or of anybody else, in this matter is to look on the question in such a way and to solve it in such a way that the best interests of the consumer are really served while, at the same time, the interests of the producer is served. That may seem a paradox, but I do not believe that this country will ever be on a sound basis if the interests of the consumers are ever considered to an extent that will make it unprofitable for people to go into production. The best thing that can be
done in the interests of the consumer is to make agriculture so productive and profitable a calling that more people will go into it and so increase production. My hon. friend raised a question that I should like to touch on because it illustrates my meaning, the question of potatoes. My hon. friend said that he wrote, I think to me, and he takes the ground-
I was answering a letter of the Agricultural Department, I do not know if it was from the minister.

My hon. friend takes the ground, and I think a great many people took the ground at that time, that in respect to the mounting price of potatoes, which were getting very high indeed, it was the business of the Government to put an embargo on the exportation of potatoes from Canada to the United States or any other country, or else that they should fix the price at a lower figure than it then was in order that the consumers might have potatoes within their reach. I want to lay this down as a maxim, and I believe it is absolutely true, that if at a time like that, when potatoes were scarce not only here, but equally so in the United States-if anything they were more scarce in the United States because they were 70,000,000 bushels short in the potato crop last year, and Cuba was also very short-we had placed an embargo on the export of potatoes the effect would have been to discourage the growing of potatoes in Canada. The growers in this country had built up, in some years at a very small margin of profit, a large business. The farmers of the province of New Brunswick had gone largely into the potato business and had built up a trade with Cuba and the Untied States which they were trying to increase, and incidentally they were supplying potatoes to consumers in this country as well. Owing not to speculation, but the shortage in United States and Cuba, the price of potatoes went up until it reached $7 a barrel. I believe that it would be a fatal mistake, however, to put an embargo on potatoes unless the necessity were extremely pressing, because the result would be the discouraging of production and a proper resentment on the part of the farmer, who would say:	Last year I raised thousands
of bushels of potatoes and sold them at a loss; this year, when I have a good crop, you deprive me of that profit which would make up for some of the losses which 1 have sustained.
Did the minister observe any resentment among the farmers of England when the British Government fixed the price of potatoes?

They did not fix a maximum price. The British Government have departed from the old established theory of not protecting the farmer. Recognizing that cheap, food at all hazards is not the best thing in the interests of the consumer, they have guaranteed a minimum price of potatoes to the farmer of $30 a ton. I fancy that if the Government had asked the Houee to sanction, a regulation guaranteeing the farmers $30 a ton for their potatoes during two years, my hon. friend would Ibe the first to say that i't was an outrage that the taxpayers should have to make up to the growers $20 a ton when their potatoes were worth only $10 a ton, as they were two years ago.

Nobody suggests the fixing of an unreasonable price. What has been argued from this side is that the Government at the beginning of the war should have fixed a minimum price for certain number of years in respect of such important foodstuffs1 as wheat and potatoes, which would have given a guarantee to the farmers, and, at the same 'time, a maximum price within which the farmers would have been obliged to sell. That would have been satisfactory to both consumer and producer.
The fixing of minimum and maximum prices upon certain commodities is a matter far more complicated and difficult than the hon. gentleman imagines, unless he has given profound study to the question.
It requires some courage to do it.

It is not altogether a question of courage; fools sometimes rush in where angels fear to tread. In Germany they rushed in with maximum prices, and they later had to go back on that policy, because of its tendency to discourage production. In Italy a similar policy also broke down. In England they have not been doing the drastic things that some people think they have been doing. They have made some mistakes. They settled upon two meatless days in each week, but they had to depart from that because of the rush on.bread and cereals. As a rule, countries which have attempted to deal in an arbitrary way with matters affected by
IMr. Burrell. ]
the laws of supply and demand have failed to attain the objects which they set out to accomplish. I believe that it would have been a mistake to place au embargo on potatoes at the time referred to, because it would have had a tendency to discourage production. It was folly for people to eat potatoes, unless they were wealthy, and used them as a luxury, at the high price which that product attained two months ago. It would have been cheaper and more economical to use rice or other commodities. As far as Canada is concerned, it was better that she should have $7 available for productive work in other directions than have a barrel of potatoes. The situation was not so severe, to my mind, as to require such a drastic remedy as the establishment of an embargo. I am speaking now of the securing of potatoes in ample time for-planting; this letter was received about four weeks ago. I had similar communications from Nova Scotia. One man wrote me that he had purchased 100 bushels for seeding purposes at $1.50 a bushel. This shows that the course suggested would not have been a wise one. Speaking generally, I think that any Government should go slowly in the matter of fixing arbitrary or maximum prices or imposing embargoes. Such courses should not be followed unless the necessities of the case are abundantly clear. My hon. friend referred to the United States. While the United States has appointed a food controller, Mr. Hoover, they have not taken any definite action; they have not even got their legislation through. The Secretary of Agriculture for the United States, with whom I have been in constant touch, kept me informed of all the proposed legislation and all their discussions, which I have followed with a great deal of interest. Mr. Houston himself said in the course of his remarks that he regarded the fixing of minimum and maximum prices as a course so important that it should only be employed as a very last resort. So far from exercising those powers in the United States,

they have not even obtained them. They are asking, however, for very large powers, and rightly so. As my hon. friend says, we are living in abnormal times, and it is well that these powers should be in existence so that the remedy may be available when it is shown to be absolutely necessary under certain conditions. After all, we are all striving for the same thing-not to discourage production. The cost of production has gone up 100, 150 and 200 per cent, and it is vital to the future of Canada that no producer be discouraged in his efforts. At the same time, I know that every member is desirous also of trying to secure the best conditions for the consuming population, who are facing hard times, and to eliminate wild speculation or manipulation-which, I think, does not exist to the extent that some people think it does. In regard to the imposition of these arbitrary measures, any Government should move very slowly if they are going to move at all.

The minister speaks of the necessity of encouraging the producer. Would he say that this was not more than a reasonable encouragement to a flour manufacturer? I Tead from the statement of the Minister of Finance on page 1957 of Hansard, where he says that the Government tax for the year 1915, when the tax was only 25 per cent of the excess profits, was $380,000 on one milling company. According to that, the excess profits of this flour milling company, after allowing for their earning the usual dividend of 7 per cent on all their investments, would be $1,520,000. Does the minister think that is an ordinary profit which ought to be encouraged? The . minister says that he is informed that the price of potatoes has gone down to $1.50 a bushel. Just the other day in my own oity 'seed potatoes cost $8 per barrel. I bought some seed potatoes for myself, and I have the bill for them.
A barrel would hold two and one-half or three bushels?
I think it is two and one-half bushels. The bill was for four barrels of potatoes for seed, $32. That does not confirm the statement of the minister.

I have been
informed that speculators are going through the different counties and buying up the crop of potatoes before they are taken out of the earth. If that be the case, the Government should stop that speculating. These speculators are also contracting for supplies of eggs, and they will control the
prices in the fall. The minister says that it is our duty to encourage the farmers; it is not the farmer who received the profit; it is those speculators who start six months ahead and gather in all that the country will grow and then fix the price. That is what is going on in Montreal, and the minister should take note of what I have just said, and if it be true, he should stop that speculation. The minister says that the dealers are now trying to sell the potatoes at $1.50 per bag. They were holding the stock, and would not give us a bushel of potatoes unless we paid $4 a bag. From twenty-five to fifty cars of potatoes were allowed to freeze on the tracks at Montreal because the dealers preferred to have them freeze to lowering the prices. I do not want to throw the blame on the Government, but they should stop this speculation for the coming crop.

I would suggest to the mayor of Montreal that he should follow the example of the mayor of New York, who now, I notice through the press of New York, is offering one dollar per bushel for all the potatoes that can be grown in the state of New York, so that he can sell direct to the consumer in New York potatoes at a reasonable price.
That suggestion might apply to the Government.

That price may seem fairly high, but that is what the mayor of New York is offering. As regards the price of coal, when hard coal is sold in the city of St. John at $14 a ton, but I would like to know, and I have not heard through this discussion, any suggestion as to how this Government can control the price of coal. We buy that coal in the United States, and regardless of what the mayor of Montreal may. say, the Government of the United States have so far not attempted to control the price of coal in that country. I am a very large buyer of coal for manufacturing institutions with which I am connected, in particular one in my own town where we use about five carloads of soft coal a week, and to-day we are advised to buy that coal now and not wait until later to buy it, because, if we do, we shall have to pay a much higher price for it. It costs us 35 cents per ton to deliver soft coal from the mines of Pennsylvania to our town, and that coal is costing us to-day in the neighbourhood of $9 a ton, over $8 anyway. How can this Government control the price and give us our coal cheaper? We used to buy that coal at $2.60 a ton. The price is controlled by the mine owners

of the United States, and the United States Government has not interfered with them in any way so that I cannot see how this Government can be held responsible for the price of coal in Canada. Will the mayor of Montreal or the hon. member for St. John tell us that the local dealers are charging exorbitant prices for coal and making exorbitant profits?

I do not think any one on this side of the House has argued that the Government can control the cost of coal in the United States, but it has been suggested by some hon. members that the dealers in Montreal and other cities have been charging more than is fair. Whether that is true or not, I do not know; my complaint has always been that the Government ought to build vessels for the coastal trade of Canada.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen need
not laugh at that. That is a pretty serious matter and ought to be attended to. I only state it because the Minister of Labour said that he would investigate the situation. Before very long, the United States Government will take charge of the coal produced in that country. We, on this side of the House, are arguing that it is the duty of this Government to take control of the necessaries of life, particularly those which are produced in Canada, such as flour

I think I understood the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite correctly and I understand that they are complaining of the price of coal in Canada. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Mr. Martin), complains that in the city of Montreal coal is being sold at too high a price. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has raised the same argument, but at the same time-and I hope it was not on account of the votes of the coal dealers-he said that he did not think that the coal dealers were charging too much.
I referred to the cost of transportation.

The price of coal is regulated by the price at the mine and the freight added to that, and I doubt if there is a coal dealer in Montreal to-day who is making over fifty cents or a dollar a ton profit on the coal he. sells. I am not speaking of the coal sold in 25 or 50 pound lots
I think we should be absolutely fair in this House whoever happens to be in power,
[Mr. Lalor.l
and not try to raise questions to influence the minds of the consumers when there is absolutely no reason for it. We have no control over the price of coal at the mines, and hon. gentlemen opposite know that just as well as we do, but the question is being discussed in this House day after day. I agree with the Minister of Agriculture that in order to get our farmers to produce more grain and grow root crops they must be encouraged, and you cannot encourage them by stepping in and controlling prices. I represent a farming constituency, and I believe the farmers of this country are entitled to the world's markets for the products of the farm. It is not all fair sailing for the farmers of this country. How about the thousands of acres of fall wheat that were ploughed up last year and which brought nothing to the farmer? How about the fall wheat in Ontario today that will not show over 50 or 60 per cent of a crop? Farmers are entitled to every cent they can get for the products of their farm.
Does my hon. friend think that they did not get enough for their cheese at 215 cents a pound?

That is a very good price, but if cheese is worth 25 cents a pound they deserve to get it. They are entitled to the price the world's markets give them for cheese. If you are going to control the product of the farm you must also control the product of the mine and factory, and if you are going to do that you must control wages.
You should not have commandeered the wheat.
Was not the wheat that was commandeered last fall in the elevators and not in the farmers' hands?
The farmers owned a great deal of what was in the elevators.

That is quite contrary to the arguments of other hon. gentlemen opposite who said that the wheat in the elevators belonged to the speculators. The hon. member for Edmonton represents a farming constituency, and he should be the first man in the House to stand up and say a good word for the farmers.

We are going to tax the people for that and we will do it.

I read a statement recently made by Mr. Hoover, controller of food in

the United States, and he is absolutely opposed to fixing a maximum price for food products. He says it has been a failure wherever it has been tried.

Does he not say that
with proper control prices could be brought down by about 60 per cent?

In England they do not fix a maximum price but a minimum price, and anything the farmer can get above that minimum he is entitled to; and that is all you can do in this country in fairness to the farmers. I want to be absolutely fair; I do not think there should be an absolute runaway market for the products of the farm, but the farmers are entitled to a fair price for their products. After listening to the arguments in this House day after day I cannot see that a food controller would do much good, or how prices could be brought down, because prices are controlled by the world's markets1.

The hon.
member has pointed to the action taken by Mayor Mitchell of New York in regard to potatoes. The Mayor of Montreal has not the same power as the Mayor of New York. Last year I suggested to the Board of control that we should vote $250,000 for the purpose of buying potatoes. We had no right to do that; it was quite illegal, but I was ready to take the responsibility in order to sell potatoes to the consumers at cost price. We did everything that was possible, so my hon. friend need not point to Mayor Mitchell as an example to me. It was illegal for us to take this action, but I thought the legislature would ratify it. The council, however, did not support me.

In regard to the potato situation my hon. friend will be glad to know that the high prices this year-and high prices are always a stimulus-have resulted in a greater acreage than last fall. I do not think there is much danger of any one speculating in the crops of the province of Quebec, because that would be an extremely wild type of speculation. I think my hon, friend can be hopeful that the efforts of the farmers and everybody else this year will result in very much more satisfactory conditions.
I understood the minister to state the .potatoes were selling in Nova Scotia at $1.50 a bushel.

Yes, near the city of Halifax. I was shown a letter only a week
or so ago in which it was said that over 100 bushels was bought for seed at $1.50.

That must have been an isolated case, because within the last twenty-four hours I have learned that a league has been formed by the citizens of Amherst to go without potatoes in June so that the people may have enough for seeding.
We may be thankful that there are enough left for seed. As it is getting late, I would suggest that we pass this item, and that the committee then rise.

The statement made by the Minister of Labour as to the information he was gathering with regard to cold storage warehouses was so diffuse and so voluminous that I was not able to gather what he was really doing, and I think we should thoroughly understand just what is being done before this item is passed.
Item stands.
